#2823. Paul George treating return to Philly as “a regular game”

Lost in the background of the highly anticipated first matchup between Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum is a return to Philadelphia for Paul George, who spent his past two seasons as a Sixer.

Both Brown and Tatum have downplayed the narrative, as hard as it is to ignore. George, who played 89 games in a Sixers uniform, is following suit.

"It's a regular game — that's how I'm treating it," he said during Boston's morning shootaround.

George said he was unsure of the reception he'd receive in his first game back to Xfinity Mobile Arena, a place where in his last appearance, he scored a series-best 23 points on 47% efficiency to go with vintage defense, forcing four Celtics turnovers and holding shooters matched up with him to 33% (5/15 FG). It played a part in Philly completing the 14th 3-1 series comeback in NBA history.

And yet, George's brief stint in Philadelphia was defined by a core group that struggled to stay on the floor at the same time, and ran into the same second round demons they've yet to exorcise since the beginning of The Process.

"Had I been here 8, 9, 10 years it'd be a different story. I was there 2 years," he said.

It's an easy narrative to shrug off for George because, over his 17 seasons, he's gone through this same thing before.

"He said he's returned to four different teams before. There's nothing new to him," Payton Pritchard said.

George had his own contentious reunion when he played against the Indiana Pacers for the first time, followed by games against the Thunder and Clippers.

George isn't the only Celtic currently on the roster to have experienced an anticipated reunion between a foundational player and the team that drafted him.

Mike Conley, a 12-year Grizzlies mainstay before the organization ended the Grit and Grind with a full scale rebuild, was showered with appreciation and given a hero's welcome from the Memphis fanbase in his first game against them in 2019.

Their experiences couldn't have been farther apart.

In the case of George, whose seven years in Indiana ended in a trade request, he first played the Pacers in Oklahoma City, struggling with foul trouble and playing just 19 minutes in an 18-point win. When he played in Indiana for the first time later that season, he was showered with boos from the moment his name was announced, and he shot just 3-of-14 for 12 points, though a late steal and two clutch free throws contributed to a 100-95 win.

"I'm happy this circus is over with. Everybody can move on," George said after his return to Indiana.

The response was different in George's next stop; he was given a tribute video and crowd ovation playing against the Thunder for the first time. Against the Clippers, a video tribute was also presented, but there was a mix of cheers and boos, a reaction he described as "stupid," though he cited no ill will towards the franchise or his time spent in Los Angeles.

"The boos, I didn't get it," he said after his first game against the Clippers. "I still don't get it when I go [back] to Indy, but it is what it is. It's sports. I look forward to next year being back here and more boos."

It's hard to say the exact response when George's name is called in the lineup introductions tonight. As the Celtics got rolling on their shootaround inside Xfinity Mobile Arena, the song "Why Can't We Be Friends" by War blared from the speakers, a tongue and cheek choice to kick off what will be one of the most watched and debated rivalry games of the season.

Perhaps it's a sign that tempers will be calm on Tuesday night. The game will be played, hands will be shaken, and hugs will be dispersed from competitor to competitor after an early November test between two Eastern Conference contenders.

#2821. Hegseth impeachment effort torpedoed in House

The House of Representatives effectively torpedoed an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth with a procedural vote on Tuesday evening.

The House, by a 211-204 margin, approved a measure that will refer the impeachment resolution to a committee.

That will leave little, if any, time for the committee and full House to act on it before Democrats take over the chamber and the Senate with a new majority in early January.

House Republican leadership had sought to kill the effort at impeachment, which was initiated Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

The vote came a week after the midterm elections, where Democrats trounced Republicans in the first congressional election since the Iran war broke out in February.

Hegseth had faced eight articles of impeachment.

Massie accused Hegseth of waging war in contravention of Congress, carrying out extrajudicial killings tied to boat strikes in the Caribbean against purported drug smugglers and suppressing free speech by targeting Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a military veteran.

Massie is a libertarian who lost his Republican primary in May after clashing with President Donald Trump.

The Kentucky Republican led a bill last year to compel the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Shortly after the vote, Trump said: "Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!"

"Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete," the president said, declaring what he said was an "EXONERATION" of Hegseth.

A Republican forced the vote on Hegseth's impeachment. All Democrats voted against referring the measure to committee.

Defense Department spokesperson Jacob Bliss said earlier in the day that Hegseth "carried out direct, lawful orders from the President to secure the nation." The impeachment effort notably focused on Hegseth, not Trump, who is responsible for launching the various military operations referred to in the articles.

Hegseth, at a press conference at the Pentagon earlier Tuesday, railed against Massie and defended his leadership in the Iran war and other military operations.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said

"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," Hegseth said. "It puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time."This is not patriotism. This is sabotage."

Trump, in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, said Hegseth "gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!"

Trump said Monday that he would stand by Hegseth even if the House impeached him. The president was impeached by the House two times during his first White House term. The Senate acquitted him in both cases.

Republicans hold a slim 218-214 majority in the House.

Some Republicans, notably including Vice President JD Vance, have directly blamed their midterm losses on the Iran war, which continues to see intermittent fighting amid an uneasy stalemate.

Neither of the two Cabinet secretaries impeached by the House has ever been removed by the Senate after a trial in that chamber.

#2818. The Rams swap out another pair of receivers following latest injury

The Los Angeles Rams have placed another receiver on injured reserve this week, as Jordan Whittington will miss at least four games with a back injury. Whittington was in line to have serious reps moving forward with Puka Nacua joining Davante Adams on IR this week, but now that opportunity will go to someone else.

Perhaps Xavier Smith, who the Rams re-signed on Tuesday in a corresponding move. Smith joins Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, and C.J. Daniels in a receivers room that looks a lot different than it did a few weeks ago.

Despite rumors like that L.A. inquired about Stefon Diggs, the Rams didn't trade for any receivers at Tuesday's deadline. This is the group they are going with.

Whittington had just four targets this season, catching two passes for 12 yards. The 22 catches for 293 yards he had as a rookie in 2024 may end up being his best career year when it's all said and done.

Instead, the Rams look to Mumpfield, last year's seventh-round pick.

Mumpfield leads all active Rams receivers with 11 catches for 162 yards. Tyler Higbee leads the team at any position among non-injured players, with 28 catches for 287 yards. Kyren Williams has 36 catches for 258 yards.

Outside of a 48-yard catch against the Broncos in which Mumpfield was practically uncovered, L.A.'s new number one receiver hasn't been productive. Aside from that play, Mumpfield has 10 catches for 114 yards and zero touchdowns in the other eight games. He had two catches for 20 yards last week.

Atwell, who the team traded for at the start of the season, has been targeted nine times in the past two games, catching four passes for 68 yards. C.J. Daniels has yet to be targeted.

So, the Rams bring back Xavier Smith, who had one target and no catches prior to his release. Smith had 18 catches for 303 yards in 2025, however.

Other notable moves on Tuesday had Josh Downs going to the Kansas City Chiefs, Keenan Allen going to the San Francisco 49ers and Brian Thomas Jr. staying with the Jasonville Jaguars. As it stands, adding Smith is the biggest move the Rams made on the NFL's trade deadline day.

Smith's biggest moment with the Rams came in the 2025 NFC Championship game when he fumbled after halftime against the Seattle Seahawks. Seattle would go on to score a touchdown and ultimately win the game. Was that play the sole reason the Rams lost? No, but it didn't help.

Entering the 2026 season, the Rams brought Smith back as their kick returner and punt returner before waiving him a few weeks into the year. Smith then went to the 49ers, who have since traded for Allen, and decided to move on from Smith. As the Rams enter Week 10, Smith is back in L.A.

Is Smith the player that the Rams needed to make up for the losses of Puka Nacua and Davante Adams? Right or wrong it's what the Rams just did, and for now, that's all they did to address their wide receiver room as another trade deadline comes to its end.

#2817. Alibaba announces plans to list T-Head, its Nvidia chip rival

Chinese tech and e-commerce giant Alibaba announced late Tuesday that the Hong Kong Stock Exchange will allow the company to spin off its semiconductor subsidiary T-Head.

To do so, Alibaba said it plans a public offering for shares of T-Head in Hong Kong, subject to approval from the exchange and the China Securities Regulatory Commission.

The filing did not disclose a date or proposed size of a listing.

Alibaba noted it had already filed confidentially on Sept. 11 to list T-Head on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

Meanwhile, Hong Kong-listed shares of Alibaba traded 1% lower Wednesday morning. The stock is down about 29% year-to-date.

In late September, Alibaba announced its next-generation AI chip, the Zhenwu V900, that it said delivers three times the performance of its predecessor, the Zhenwu M890 released in May.

Alibaba is one of several Chinese companies, including Huawei, developing homegrown semiconductors to power artificial intelligence, amid growing U.S. restrictions on China's ability to access the chips.

Short seller Culper Research alleged in May that Alibaba was able to obtain restricted Nvidia chips by indirectly financing entities in Southeast Asia. Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

News of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy involved with one of those entities has dragged down the stock to its lowest valuation since late March, weighing on the overall U.S. stock market.

Amid the tech stock volatility, U.S.-based AI giant Anthropic said in an updated filing Tuesday that it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share.

Trading on the Nasdaq is expected to begin on Nov. 19, people familiar with the details told CNBC. They were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Chinese tech stocks have underperformed their U.S. peers, despite investor excitement last year around AI breakthroughs by DeepSeek.

Baidu has reportedly delayed the listing of its AI chip entity Kunlunxin, as has Chinese memory chip company YMTC, according to news reports this month. Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment.

In the last few months, China's financial regulators have increased their scrutiny on tech IPOs and the rush of capital into the sector.

—CNBC's Fred Imbert, Ashley Capoot and Leslie Picker contributed to this report

#2816. 10 Takeaways: Avalanche’s Veterans Made Their Presence Felt in Toronto

What a night for some of the Avalanche's most experienced players. Gabe Landeskog, Devon Toews, Brock Nelson, and Nazem Kadri were all instrumental in helping Colorado open its road trip with a 6-3 victory over the Toronto Maple Leafs.

Read NextPostgame Reaction: Devon Toews Is Giving the Avalanche Another Offensive Weapon

1. Landeskog has had an interesting start to the season. He looked slow during the early portions of the schedule but started to pick things up offensively from time to time. In recent games, it feels like the captain has found all sorts of ways to be effective. His fight against Moritz Seider on Saturday at Ball Arena was one of the highlights of the night. Three days later, he scored twice, including the game-winner, to lead Colorado past Toronto.

Landeskog now has seven goals and 12 points in 19 games. He's on pace for more than 50 points over a full season, which would be massive for him at this stage of his career.

2. How about that pass from Kadri on Landeskog's game-winning goal? It helped that none of Toronto's defenders challenged him behind the net, but Kadri still had to thread the needle. He sent a pass through the blue paint to find Landeskog in front, with the puck slipping between goalie Sergei Bobrovsky and defenseman Darren Raddysh.

It came just 51 seconds after Jack Roslovic tied the game at 3-3. That's an impressive response, and Kadri deserves credit for the helper.

3. I highlighted this in my postgame reaction, but Toews' offensive production has been a major factor in Colorado getting more out of its defensemen. Head coach Jared Bednar separated Toews and Cale Makar shortly after Josh Manson's injury, putting Toews with Sam Malinski and Makar with Brett Kulak.

The results have been encouraging. Toews has continued producing, Makar has picked up his offensive game, and Malinski has started contributing more consistently. It's given Colorado a different look on the back end without sacrificing the offense it expects from its top blueliners.

4. Oh yeah, the Avs won 6-3 in Toronto, and Toews finished the night with a +5 rating.

5. Malinski didn't do much offensively when the season began. He was held without a point through his first five games, which included a healthy scratch in Calgary. Since then, he's slowly worked his way back into a rhythm.

In his last eight games, Malinski has six assists. He still hasn't found the back of the net, but he's getting more comfortable and showing more of the offensive instincts from a season ago. He finished with an assist and was +3 against the Maple Leafs on Tuesday night.

6. Continuing with the veteran contributions, Nelson scored Colorado's first goal on a play that started on Jaden Schwartz' stick. Nelson buried his fifth of the season to tie things at 1-1 after the Avalanche fell behind early. It was an important response from a team that hasn't always done a great job of recovering after surrendering the first goal on the road.

7. Blackwood has to make that save against Easton Cowan late in the second period. There's no sugarcoating that. He has to do a better job of covering his post. It was a shot from a tight angle, and the Colorado netminder left enough room for Cowan to squeeze it through.

Aside from that, it was another solid performance. Blackwood made 28 saves, improving to 10-3-1 on the season. He's now the third goaltender in the NHL to reach double-digit wins.

8. I'm sure many of you remember how heavily Blackwood was scrutinized after Colorado's previous game against Toronto exactly a month earlier. He surrendered three goals on four shots in the second period alone, and the Avalanche went on to lose 6-3 at home. Following that performance, Blackwood was 2-2 in four starts with an .867 save percentage. There were legitimate questions about whether he had what it takes to be Colorado's No. 1 option.

Since then, he's gone 8-1-1 in 10 starts, with a .913 save percentage and a shutout. That's an incredible response and speaks to his resilience. It also helps that Bednar continued to believe in him and allowed him to play through those early-season inconsistencies. Blackwood has rewarded that confidence.

9. This feels like the first time Blackwood is truly being tested as the guy in Colorado. Bednar went through a similar process with Alexandar Georgiev in the past, allowing him to establish himself as the primary option.

I don't envision Blackwood getting overplayed in quite the same way, especially with Scott Wedgewood more than capable of handling a larger share of the workload despite his slow start.

But it's important for Blackwood to play a lot. He worked extremely hard this summer, and Bednar knows what he's put into getting himself ready for this opportunity. Blackwood hasn't played a ton of games in recent years, and this is his first real chance to establish himself as a go-to starter. I appreciate Bednar challenging him, and I like seeing Blackwood respond the way he has.

It's hard to believe that Blackwood has never reached 30 wins in a season. The fact that he's already at 10 and we're not yet a quarter into 2026-27 is a great sign towards him reaching that mark.

10. Kudos to the fourth line for doing its part in creating the play that led to Toews' goal. Logan O'Connor and Parker Kelly continue to show great chemistry as wingers on the same line. The Avs really missed having those two together during the first month or so of the season.

10 Takeaways: Avalanche's Power Play Held Them Back Again (+)

#2814. ‘Thank goodness he’s on our team’: Cooper Flagg makes history, Dallas Mavericks keep stacking wins

With the Dallas Mavericks down 13 points late in the first half on the second night of a back-to-back, Monday night at American Airlines Center looked very much like a schedule loss. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving had other ideas, though, as they combined for 78 points, fueling Dallas past the Indiana Pacers in a wild finish, 125-122.

The win was the Mavericks' third straight and moved Dallas to 7-4 on the season. It also put the Mavs three games over .500 for the first time since March 1, 2025, a date that feels a lot longer ago than it actually is for anyone who has lived through the last two years of Mavericks basketball.

Think about where this franchise was not long ago. The Luka Doncic trade. Irving's torn ACL. A 26-56 season and back-to-back years without a playoff appearance. Oddsmakers set Dallas' win total at 34.5 before this season, and after an opening stretch that included Houston, San Antonio and Oklahoma City, a lot of people expected the Mavs to be scrapping just to stay afloat by mid-November.

Instead, the Mavs are stacking wins, Flagg looks like an MVP candidate in year two, and Irving looks like his old self before the ACL injury happened. Most importantly, the way the Mavs are winning these games feels sustainable. Here are some of the biggest storylines from Monday night's thriller.

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Cooper Flagg #32 of the Dallas Mavericks dunks during the first half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Flagg was good in the first half, but he was on an entirely different level in the second.

The 19-year-old star scored 30 of his season-high 43 points after halftime, including 14 on 6-of-6 shooting in the third quarter and 16 more in the fourth. He finished 16-of-25 from the field, 3-of-6 from 3-point range and a perfect 8-of-8 at the free-throw line, adding 10 rebounds, six assists, three steals and a block for his fourth straight double-double.

Flagg became just the second teenager in NBA history to post at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a game, joining Kevin Durant, who put up 42 points, 13 rebounds and six assists in the final game of his rookie season with Seattle in 2008. Per StatMuse, add the three steals, and Flagg is the first teenager ever with a 40-10-5-3 line.

It was also his fifth career 40-point game, as many as the next two teenagers on that list combined (LeBron James with three and Anthony Edwards with two). His 14th career 30-point game moved him into second place for the most by a player under 20, behind only James, and his seventh 35-point game tied James for the most by a teenager. And keep in mind, Flagg doesn't turn 20 until Dec. 21.

Mavericks head coach Dusty May pointed to how complete Flagg's scoring package has become.

"He gets to the rim," May said in his postgame media availability. "I think him almost being a left-handed player in the paint certainly helps. He's a great left-footed jumper, left-handed finisher. Then he's able to square in the air from 15, 17 feet. … The last couple of games, he's made some threes and he's making all of his free throws. That's how you put up the 43 points, where you do a little bit of everything."

It's almost unreal just how good Flagg already is, and May is just happy he's on his roster and not having to gameplan against him.

"He affects the game in so many ways and he makes the right plays as far as passing," May said. "Thank goodness he's on our team. It's unbelievable that he's a 19-year-old doing this."

Flagg's deadly midrange shot, which he worked on all offseason, is paying off in a big way, especially in clutch situations, where he leads the league in clutch points.

"I think just being able to get to my spots at a higher level and being more comfortable with that has allowed me to take a little bit of load off my body," Flagg said. "Just kind of stopping short, raising up over people. It's taxing going downhill all the way to the rim and trying to finish over seven-footers all night, every night. … Just trusting the work, trusting the spot work that I put in all summer long."

Through 11 games, the reigning Rookie of the Year is averaging 25.9 points, 6.9 rebounds, 6.9 assists and 2.2 steals per game. Again, given everything Mavs fans have been through over the last 21 months, this sort of euphoric rise back to genuine happiness watching these games is hard to believe.

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Kyrie Irving #11 of the Dallas Mavericks celebrates after scoring a three point basket during the second half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Flagg was the closer on Monday night, but Irving was arguably the reason Dallas was still in the game in those closing moments.

Playing the second night of a back-to-back for the first time this season, a day after logging 28 minutes in a 130-93 win over Brooklyn, Irving poured in 35 points in a season-high 38 minutes. He knocked down a season-high seven 3-pointers on 10 attempts, went 3-of-3 at the line and finished a game-best plus-29.

After missing 19 months with the torn ACL he suffered in March 2025, Irving said he told his teammates in the locker room after Sunday's win that he planned to play.

"When you're in a combative sport such as basketball, some days are going to feel good, some days aren't, especially coming off an injury or a long period of time," Irving said. "So I just had to get my body back used to being in the flow of the game. … I was just feeling great, and just coming in to today."

May, who said plus-minus is often overblown in a one-game sample, made an exception for Irving in this one.

"His plus-29 tonight was very indicative of how important he is," May said. "When we were struggling to make shots in the first half, we thought we were generating really good looks. We just looked a little bit flat. I thought Kyrie's shot-making just kind of righted the ship for us."

It's still early, but seeing Irving look this healthy and proving to be a seamless fit next to Flagg bodes well for what this team can accomplish this year. Perhaps the last two years of the basketball injury gods punishing the Mavs will result in some good injury luck the rest of this season.

DALLAS, TEXAS – NOVEMBER 9: Cooper Flagg #32 of the Dallas Mavericks celebrates with teammate Kyrie Irving #11 of the Dallas Mavericks after scoring a basket during the second half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The most encouraging part of all of this is just how naturally Flagg and Irving shared the scoring load against Indiana. The two combined for 26 fourth-quarter points, including Dallas' first 13 of the period, and May said neither player blinks when the play call goes to the other.

"We're coming out of a timeout, we may draw up a play for one of them just because the other one might have an All-League defender on him, or whatever the case, and they never roll their eyes," May said. "They know when we're going to one of the two, the other one's very, very supportive because they have that much respect for each other."

Irving, an established champion who has shared the floor with more than a few superstars over his 15-year career, is grateful that he's able to be Flagg's teammate, despite the two players being on different ends of their careers.

"We keep calling him a teenager, but he plays way beyond his years. We've got to give him his flowers," Irving said. "Most young guys will probably move away from that contact, but it seems like this newer generation that's coming into our league, they fear nothing. And I think he falls right in line with that. So grateful to have him on the wing with me."

Those feelings are mutual for Flagg: "Just having [Kyrie] out there, his gravity opening the floor for everybody else, it makes my life so much easier."

Washington #25 of the Dallas Mavericks celebrates a three point basket during the second half against the Indiana Pacers at American Airlines Center on November 9, 2026 in Dallas, Texas. It wasn't pretty at the end, but it didn't have to be for the Mavs to come up with another win. That's one thing that's been so encouraging about this fast start to the season. Dallas is finding different ways to win, whether it's pretty or not.

Indiana's Pascal Siakam torched Dallas for 26 first-half points on 8-of-9 shooting, but the Mavs adjusted their help defense after the break and held him to just three points on 1-of-7 shooting the rest of the way. The Pacers took a 66-56 lead into halftime and a 93-90 lead into the fourth before Flagg buried a 26-foot pull-up 3 to tie it. Irving's 23-footer with 9:36 left put Dallas in front for good.

Leading 125-122 with a chance to put the game on ice, PJ Washington missed a pair of free throws with four seconds left, and Caleb Martin bailed everyone out by stealing Andrew Nembhard's inbounds pass to Siakam with 0.9 seconds remaining. Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle was adamant that Martin fouled Siakam on that final play, but judging from the replays, it looked like Martin got all ball before ever making any contact with Siakam.

It obviously would've been nice for Washington to sink at least one of those free throws to avoid that last-second drama, but again, the Mavs keep finding different ways to win. How many times over the past two years have we seen a game like that end in a loss for Dallas?

"We haven't earned anything in this league yet," Irving said. "We consistently do it every night, and that's how you build your identity in this league and you earn your respect. We try not to put the cart before the horse."

With that being said, though, Mavs fans have earned the right to enjoy this start and, dare I say, dream big again. After two years of nothing but gut punches, a 7-4 start built on a generational teenager, a healthy veteran star and a team that genuinely seems to like playing together is a foundation Mavs fans have been waiting on.

Irving acknowledged the preseason doubt, saying the team heard "a lot of the noise" and chose not to let outside voices into the locker room. If he keeps playing like prime Kyrie, though, and if Flagg keeps rewriting the record books at this current pace, those voices of doubt are going to continue to get a whole lot quieter.

The Mavericks will now hit the road for a big three-game trip that will show just how real this start is, beginning Thursday against the Minnesota Timberwolves at Target Center at 7 p.m. CT. Dallas then visits the Cleveland Cavaliers on Nov. 14 and the Boston Celtics on Nov. 15.

#2812. The AI ‘credit card’ is getting costlier as CoreWeave bond yield tops 16%

Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.

That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."

That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.

"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."

Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.

CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.

Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.

The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.

Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.

None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.

The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.

The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.

Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.

"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.

Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.

As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.

-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

#2811. Bessent reportedly moved to military base over Iranian threats on his life

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reportedly moved from his Washington, D.C., home to a military base due to Iranian threats on his life.

The New York Times, citing officials familiar with the matter, said that U.S. officials had concluded Iranian plotting against current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage.

Separately, Reuters reported that the severity of the threats against Bessent was not immediately clear.

Bessent has led "Operation Economic Outcast," a Treasury campaign launched in August to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and other financial measures, in addition to the U.S. military actions.

The Times reported that Bessent's role in that campaign has made him one of the Trump administration officials Iran most wanted to target.

The move comes as the Department of Justice Department said late Tuesday that three Iranian nationals had been indicted on terrorism-related charges.

The department said the three were allegedly involved in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States.

The alleged plots included a September 2026 attack targeting RAF Fairford in the U.K., where U.S. military personnel were stationed.

"Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

Earlier in October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was involved in the incident at RAF Fairford that led to the arrest of five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi then rejected the allegation, writing on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."

RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, is a key U.S. Air Force operating location in Europe and has supported deployments of American strategic bombers and other aircrafts.

Separately, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly said military action against Iran may not be necessary if economic sanctions and Washington's naval blockade are working.

On Monday, President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History."

"We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict," Trump added.

Asked Tuesday why he would not simply declare an end to the Iran war, Trump said he wanted to ensure U.S. allies in the region were "not hurt" and that there was a "long term solution.

However, Iranian officials have denied that negotiations are underway. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said claims that talks were continuing were aimed at "easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices."

Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude prices edged higher during Wednesday's Asia trading session, at about $92 and $86 per barrel, respectively.

#2809. Views from the Game: Rockets defeat Nuggets 110-100; TDS speaks with Kevin Durant, Alperen Sengun

The Houston Rockets faced the Denver Nuggets in unfamiliar territory on Monday. The Rockets entered Monday night's game on their first two-game losing streak of the season after their 102-99 loss to the Phoenix Suns on Saturday.

In that game, the Rockets struggled from the field as the Suns led by double digits in the first quarter. The Rockets eventually got back in the game and even took a six-point lead at one point in the second half. Still, even a fourth-quarter resurgence from Alperen Sengun, who struggled the first three quarters, wasn't enough to keep the Rockets from dropping their second straight game.

The Rockets welcomed the Nuggets, who are coming off a win down in Mexico City over the Los Angeles Clippers. The Rockets have been without Steven Adams and Clint Capela for several games and also added Oscar Tshiebwe to their injury report with an illness. That means the Rockets will be without all three of their backup centers, leaving Sengun as the only active center for Monday's game.

Ime Udoka did mention how both Steven Adams and Clint Capela are targeting the upcoming road trip, specifically the Washington and Miami games, as possible return dates. That would be a welcome sight for a Rockets team that currently ranks 12th in rebounding after being near or at the top every season of Ime Udoka's Rockets tenure.

The Rockets got off to a fast start, led by Durant, who made his first three shots, including one from beyond the arc. Durant was as aggressive in the first quarter as he has been in several games. The quarter was back and forth, as neither team could get much separation.

The Nuggets started to take advantage of the Rockets' lack of depth at center as Jokic went to work once Sengun went to the bench. However, the Rockets put together a good finish to the quarter, and a Tari Eason 3-pointer put them up 32-24 at the end of the first quarter. Durant led all scorers with 11 points in the first 12 minutes.

The Rockets carried that momentum into the second quarter, scoring the first 11 points and building a lead of as much as 19. The Rockets played with much more force and composure than in their first half against the Suns. The Rockets had 13 assists out of their first 20 made baskets. The Rockets maintained the lead, taking a 54-40 lead into halftime.

The third quarter saw the Nuggets cut the lead to under double digits early as they started the quarter on fire from the field. The Rockets, meanwhile, saw their shooting fall off a cliff, starting 2-for-14 from the field as the Nuggets came back from an early 18-point deficit to tie the game at 5:02.

That's when Marcus Smart and Tari Eason entered the game, and the Rockets' defensive intensity immediately rose. The Rockets strung together good defensive possessions that led to easy baskets and pushed the lead back to nine at 71-62. Despite a rough start to the quarter, the Rockets led 77-68 heading into the fourth quarter.

In the fourth quarter, both teams played at a high level for the first time. On one end, Sengun scored in the paint; on the other, Jamal Murray could not miss from mid-range. The Rockets had a slim six-point lead midway through the fourth quarter.

That's when Sengun took over: he not only scored in the paint to give the Rockets a 98-90 lead, but he also assisted on the next two baskets, helping the Rockets put the game away with a 110-100 win. The win snapped the Rockets' first two-game losing streak of the season.

After the game, Ime Udoka, Kevin Durant, and Alperen Sengun spoke to the media. Udoka said the Rockets did a much better job taking care of the basketball and distributing it, and that they finished with 29 assists. SB Nation asked Durant whether it is easier to figure out the defense when he's initiating the offense.

Sengun helped close out the Nuggets with his own great passing and running the pick-and-roll with Durant. Here are both players praising each other's games after last night's win.

The Rockets now begin preparing for their old nemesis, Steph Curry and the Golden State Warriors, who come to town Wednesday with an 8-3 record and have won their last eight games.

#2808. Nvidia's Huang tries to project 'business as usual' in return to office after affair revelation

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang walked into the chipmaker's Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday and conducted his regular morning meeting with top-level executives, people familiar with the meeting told CNBC.

On Sunday, Huang had disclosed an extramarital affair to employees.

Huang kicked off the closed-door gathering by addressing his infidelity and sharing how sorry he was to his staff, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. They said Huang didn't take any questions and quickly pivoted to business and top agenda items of the day.

The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings just one week ahead of the company's quarterly earnings report.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

People inside the artificial intelligence chip giant said Huang tried to project "business as usual," even as the probe moved forward into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The CEO was in a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, according to The Financial Times.

Sentiment toward Jensen Huang shifted on Sunday after the 63-year-old revealed in an email to employees that he had an affair, though he did not disclose with whom he had the relationship.

"I know an apology cannot undo what I have done," he wrote. "I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust." Nvidia's board opened an investigation and hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the probe on Tuesday.

Employees inside the firm described the mood to CNBC as "sad." One employee told CNBC that they were shocked by Jensen Huang's revelations.

People also told CNBC that longtime employees viewed Jensen Huang as an idol who could do no wrong and thought of him as a guiding light. Many employees at the company are also struggling to come to grips with the CEO's actions, the people said.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 to build graphics processing units for video game graphics. In recent years, the company has become synonymous with the AI boom, powering the technology that underpins large language models and the massive data center buildout.

A central figure in the development of every AI layer, the Nvidia CEO is also a key voice in Washington, even accompanying President Donald Trump on his trip to China in May. In September, Jensen Huang and his wife were pictured at the same table as Chinese President Xi Jinping for the White House's state dinner.

The news of the CEO's affair has drawn increased scrutiny on his continued support for more AI chip sales to China.

#2806. Raiders offer blunt reasoning to holding onto Maxx Crosby at trade deadline

The Raiders had a pretty good idea who would take Kirk Cousins' place if they traded him Tuesday. They used the first pick in the draft on Fernando Mendoza, watched him get better by the week in practice and came to the conclusion he was ready for his shot.

Now try having that same conversation about Maxx Crosby.

Who takes his place on Sunday? For that matter, who takes it next September?

Somewhere in the answers to those questions is the explanation for how the Raiders could send their starting quarterback to the Vikings and hold on to their best defensive player at the same trade deadline.

Which is why the Raiders said yes to a trade offer for Cousins, but were not interested in dealing Crosby, whom they believe is a big part of their future and an asset that can help the transition to Mendoza.

Las Vegas Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby warms up before a game against the New England Patriots in Foxborough, Mass., Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

"We're always going to make the best decision for the Raiders," is how general manager John Spytek put it bluntly.

And it's likely part of the reason NFL teams showed little interest in trading for Crosby on Tuesday. Multiple league sources indicated there was minimal talk regarding Crosby, and indicated the Raiders had something to do with that by making it clear they wanted to keep him.

That gave potential suitors little reason to believe a phone call would get them very far.

"We say no a lot more than we say yes," Spytek said.

Crosby had been sending much the same message about wanting to remain in Las Vegas as the Raiders did about keeping him.

Even after everything that happened last March, he has continued to express his desire to spend his entire career with the Raiders. He remains under contract, is beloved by the fan base and, most important to the people making the decision, figures prominently in how they see this team coming together over the next few years.

Fernando Mendoza of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before a game against the San Francisco 49ers in Santa Clara, Calif., Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Getty Images

Cousins arrived in Las Vegas under an entirely different set of circumstances. His job was to give the Raiders a veteran quarterback they could win with while Mendoza learned Klint Kubiak's offense. There was always going to be an expiration date on that arrangement. The question was whether it would come sometime next spring or on a Tuesday afternoon in November.

Cousins held up his end. The Raiders won their first three games with him under center. They took the Chiefs and Bills down to the wire. And at 4-5, there was a reasonable argument for sticking with a veteran who still gave them a chance to play meaningful games in December.

Most of what he's done to make his case has happened on a practice field, out of public view. The rookie has been shining there, and the Raiders have seen enough to feel good about putting the offense in his hands. They understand there will be a learning curve. They're ready to live with it.

Kirk Cousins of the Las Vegas Raiders celebrates a touchdown against the San Francisco 49ers in Santa Clara, Calif., Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Getty Images

And really, what more could they ask Cousins to do? He gave Mendoza nine games to watch how a veteran prepares for a defense, handles a bad series and comes back to work after a tough loss. What Mendoza needs now is the experience of throwing a costly interception himself, walking back to the sideline and figuring out how to go score on the next drive. Cousins could only take him so far with that part of the job.

For all the attention on what a contender might be able to do with him down the stretch, the Raiders are entitled to consider what they can do with him, too. They have a first-year head coach and a rookie quarterback about to make his first start. There's something to be said for having a player of Crosby's caliber around while those two find their footing, especially one who wants to be here to see where it goes.

From the day the Raiders drafted Mendoza, they could picture their next good team with him at quarterback. By Tuesday, they were ready to start finding out how soon he could get them there.

When they picture that same team on defense, they still see Crosby coming off the edge.

#2805. What We Learned from the Spurs win over the Suns

It's hard not to feel like you're watching a mirage during some of these games. The level of play is excellent and the bits and pieces you might be tempted to pick at are scarce. The wins are piling up. The vibes are good. Everything is going according to plan. Nothing to see here…right?

Right! Look, I'm not going to even try to play devil's advocate here. No one wants to be the guy pointing at the Alien dropping 40 and 11 over 25 minutes and saying, "actually, this is bad." If that's a take you'd like to read then I can assure the internet is full of people willing to take you up on the offer. For my part, and if you've come to this website today, I'm assuring you, I genuinely find it hard to think of a less interesting angle to come at this from.

Victor Wembanyama is simply brilliant. He's been brilliant, he's brilliant now, and he only seems to be getting more brillianter as we go along. Twelve of his fifteen made shots on Monday were dunks or layups, and nine of those were dunks. Four different teammates threw him an alley-oop. The Spurs are running a dizzying array of different motions that all end up at the same destination, which is a Wembanyama dunk. The threes, instead of feeling like something he has to do to open up the lane, now just arrive in the natural rhythm of the game. He made two threes all night, a digestif tacked on at the end of a satisfying meal.

Vic even hit a Dream Shake in the middle of the 2nd quarter that left me staring off in the distance in disbelief.

I sometimes try to avoid writing about the Victor Wembanyama of it all when I do these because it feels too easy. What did we learn from the Spurs win? They still have the best player on the planet and he helps a lot. Case closed. To his credit, he goes out of his way to make ignoring him next to impossible.

The problem, if there is one, is that regular season basketball does actually seem easy for him at this point. That's not a mirage. I have no doubt about how hard he's worked to achieve the level he's currently operating on, but that doesn't change the fact that watching him dismantle the average NBA team every other night doesn't look very challenging. He's like Will Hunting ranting at Professor Lambeau about how easy it is to solve those supposedly impossible graph theory equations.

Victor's ascension this season is impressive, and I want to do my best to appreciate the casual brilliance we are privy to on a regular basis, but that greatness comes at a cost, and that cost is a raised ceiling. I simply don't care that he can drop 50 on the Mavs or 40 on the Suns. I don't care that he can snuff out the Blazers. I'm sure there will be another jaw-dropping stat line on Wednesday when he plays the Bulls, and I'm sure it will be met with another polite nod from me.

None of this is his fault, mind you. The schedule is the schedule and the teams are the teams. He's taking care of business, and that's all you can really ask of him.

I guess I've just spent the last nine games of this winning streak telling myself I still don't know what I'm looking at and I really believe anyone who tells you they do is lying. The ease with which they are winning these games is real. Every conclusion we draw from it…well, that's a little more hazy. I try to grab on to things I know. "The Spurs are Good." "The Suns are Bad." "Wemby is Tall," and project out from there but I end up feeling like I'm chasing the ghost of a conclusion. The idea of a resolution instead of an actual one.

This is a champagne problem at most. Like, what, I'm having a bad time because I can't tell if the Spurs are great, really great, or generationally amazing? A few years ago we were sitting through a sixteen-game losing streak and then an eighteen-game one, on our way to the lottery again and again. Now I'm hemming and hawing because our first brush with success last spring has got me feeling antsy.

The thing I'm dancing around here is that the Finals loss is an albatross around our necks that we're just going to have to wear. There's no two ways about it. I'm encouraged by the things I'm seeing from this new three-guard- Hydra, but I won't feel comfortable until I know it can outscore Jalen Brunson when he's going Nuclear. I love that Victor seems more calm and assured in his decision making, but I still have nightmares about KAT finding a way to neutralize him. Every time we race out to a lead this season, my brain remembers the blown leads in June.

The context of the past clouds everything from the present and I don't think there's an easy fix for that feeling. It shouldn't sully our enjoyment of the current moment, but it does ground the results in a certain reality.

All of this is certainly real enough, but none of it really matters.

I don't feel qualified to talk about what Dylan Harper is doing. It's a level of basketball that I recognize as great but have difficulty quantifying, because my analysis tends to err on the side of "oh my God, how did he do that?" Nuance exits the room when he has the ball in his hands. There is a grace and fluidity to his game that is hypnotic, whether he's getting to the basket with relative ease or casually spinning into a midrange jumper. I don't know how to say this as a compliment, but it's fascinatingly boring to watch. He's operating at breakneck speed but still in complete control, sort of like how F1 cars can look a little blah during a race until you blink and realize they're going like 200 mph.

The caveat with Dylan is, obviously, his youth. It's simultaneously the most exciting and frustrating thing about him. That control I just alluded to can prove elusive sometimes. Sometimes he seems almost like he's just watching the game happen to him and forgets that he's more than capable of grabbing the reins. He started the game last night a little bit adrift. Whether that's a byproduct of the three-guard lineup's growing pains or him simply sitting back and watching Wemby cook like the rest of us, he was kind of invisible, and a guy like Harper just shouldn't be invisible. After the game, Mitch talked about calling him out specifically during a timeout in the 3rd, and that wake-up call seemed to snap him back into place. He absolutely torched the Suns in that 3rd quarter, going 6-of-8 from the field and effectively putting the game out of reach after Phoenix briefly tried to make a run. He is, without a doubt, the 2nd best player on the team from a talent perspective, and that this already kinda feels indisputable is the most shocking thing of all.

It would've been so easy to just write off De'Aaron Fox this season, as evidenced by that fact that so many people did, in fact, write him off. But he's been really fun to watch so far this year. I love the way he fits into the similar but different skill sets of our guards, and he seems a little more freed up now that Harper and Castle can take on more responsibility. He's still so fast and he still has great vision, and last night he finished with 15 points, six assists and nine rebounds. His chemistry with Wembanyama has only gotten better, with four of those six assists going to Wemby, and their propensity for lobs and oops of all types seems to have rubbed off on everyone around them. It's kind of exactly what you would want from a veteran leader in the starting lineup. Everyone else is right though, the Spurs probably should've just shipped him last summer because everyone on Twitter was mad.

Are you ever going to stop having an existential crisis about the Spurs this season?

Are you kidding? My entire brand is "existential crisis about the Spurs." What would I even write about if not that?

You could analyze the gameplay? Trending stats? Maybe break down different plays the offense runs? Talk about defensive schemes?

You sound insane right now. Completely bonkers.

I just think people come here trying to figure out what they learned from the game and you're only even talking about the journey through the dark night of the soul you went through on a random Monday. We're eleven games into the season! You don't want to, like, build to that?

Shooters shoot. I'm not going to lie to the readers about the fact that I can't sit still and watch Wembanyama dunk on dudes without stressing about the inexorable march of time or whatever.

I'm not asking you to lie, but also, like, can you not sit still and just watch Wembanyama dunk on dudes without stressing about the inexorable march of time or whatever? Like, are you incapable of doing that?

#2804. Vikings bring Kirk Cousins back to Minnesota

Guess who’s back? Back again? Kirk-o’s back. Tell a friend.

#2801. Kirk Cousins can become the first quarterback to play an 18-game regular season

With the Raiders trading him to the Vikings, Kirk Cousins has an opportunity to do something no quarterback has done before: Play 18 games in a single regular season.

Cousins has already started nine games this season for the Raiders, who have not had their bye. He’s now joining the Vikings, who have nine games left on their schedule because they have already had their bye. If Cousins plays every game the rest of the season, he’ll have played 18 regular-season games.

Since the NFL expanded the regular season to 17 games over 18 weeks in 2021, four players have played 18 games in a regular season because they moved from a team that hadn’t had its bye to a team that had: Rashid Shaheed and Dre’Mont Jones in 2025, Mike Williams in 2024 and Leonard Williams in 2023.

The NFL record for games in a season is actually 19, set by four members of the Frankford Yellow Jackets, a team that routinely played more games than other NFL teams in the 1920s. But in the modern era, 18 games has been the most a player could conceivably pay, and Cousins, as a starting quarterback, may become the most noteworthy player to do it.

#2800. “Lack Of Connectivity”: Jon Scheyer Offers No Filter After Duke Makes Headlines For All The Wrong Reasons vs Michigan State

Duke walked into Chicago ranked No. 2, with one of the deepest rosters in college basketball and a coach who said he wanted his team tested. Hours later, the Blue Devils had been tested, and they did not pass. For the first time this season, Duke lost, and Jon Scheyer did not try to dress it up.

After Duke fell to Michigan State 79-73, Scheyer admitted his team had been outplayed.

"They outplayed us in every facet of the game, I thought. Our lack of connectivity on offense was not good enough. We're going to fix it. We have things to address and we'll fix it. It's a long season ahead," he said.

The final score told only part of the story. Michigan State never allowed Duke to take the lead at any point in the 40 minutes, keeping the Blue Devils chasing from the opening tip.

And the Spartans made sure that chase started early. They made their first four shots and ripped off an 11-2 run, forcing Scheyer to call a timeout just 2:33 into the game. Duke turned the ball over four times in the first three minutes, and nothing seemed to fall.

The Blue Devils missed 11 of their first 13 shots and went 0-of-8 from three-point range to start. By halftime, Duke had made just 7-of-27 shots, while Michigan State carried a 34-25 lead into the break.

That early struggle eventually became the bigger problem Scheyer pointed to: Duke's lack of connectivity on offense. The Blue Devils had looked smooth in their first two games, averaging 98.5 points while shooting a combined 55%. Against Michigan State, however, the ball stopped moving with the same rhythm. Duke finished with 13 turnovers and shot 33.3% overall (20 of 60) and about 24% from three.

John Blackwell led Duke with 17 points, but it took him 16 shots to get there. Deron Rippey Jr., meanwhile, went 1 of 5.

Michigan State deserves plenty of credit for that offensive breakdown. The Spartans played the kind of defense that makes even a talented team look lost. Jordan Scott, a 6-foot-8 sophomore, recorded six of Michigan State's eight blocks, doing so after never having more than two in a game. Five of those came in the first half alone.

While Scott protected the paint, Jeremy Fears Jr. took charge on the other end. He finished with 18 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds. He already had eight assists by halftime and scored or assisted on 22 of Michigan State's 34 first-half points. The Spartans' bench also outscored Duke's 35-28.

Simply put, Michigan State brought more physicality and intensity. Duke struggled to match it, and that difference showed throughout the night.

The Blue Devils also made their task harder at the free-throw line. They went 26 of 37, leaving 11 points on the table in a game they lost by six. Patrick Ngongba II, who finished with 11 points, was just 7 of 13 from the stripe.

To be fair, Duke did win some of the other battles. It outrebounded Michigan State 40-38, including 18-9 on the offensive glass, and scored 14 second-chance points compared to the Spartans' six. But when a team struggles to make shots in the half court, extra possessions can only do so much.

In fact, Scheyer had expected Michigan State to present a different kind of challenge. Before the game, he said, "There's no question Michigan State is gonna test us in ways we haven't seen yet."

The Spartans certainly delivered. Duke did make a late push, with a 12-6 burst cutting the lead to 73-68 on two Caleb Foster free throws with 2:03 left. But Scott answered with a driving layup, and Fears sealed the win at the free-throw line.

For Michigan State, the victory carried plenty of meaning. It was Tom Izzo's first win over Scheyer and the program's first victory against Duke since December 1, 2020. Izzo now has a 4-15 record against the Blue Devils.

For Duke, the focus now shifts to what comes next. The Blue Devils host SIU Edwardsville on Friday before welcoming Illinois to Cameron Indoor Stadium. Within the next month, they will also face No. 1 Florida and No. 4 UConn.

Those games will give Scheyer plenty of opportunities to address the issues he saw in Chicago. If Duke finds its offensive rhythm again, Tuesday could become just an early bump in a long season. If not, the headlines from Chicago may only be the beginning.

#2799. How does ILB Daiyan Henley fit into Broncos’ long-term plans?

The Denver Broncos trade with the Los Angeles Chargers for inside linebacker Daiyan Henley was one that few of us were expecting with all eyes watching for running back news. But it was an underrated move that may pay big dividends down the road.

Henley is in the final year of rookie deal, so he'll clearly be looking at an extension from the Broncos now that they've spent two picks to acquire him. Where does that leave Justin Strnad and Alex Singleton after this season? From a cap savings perspective, the green dot holding veteran Singleton would be the odd man out next March. Denver would save $4M in cap with $5M in dead money. Plus Strnad is three years younger and would incur $7M in dead money and no cap savings.

The move seems to signal the teams willingness to move on from Singleton either next March or after his contract runs its course through 2027.

Additionally, Henley has worn the green dot for the Chargers the last several seasons and is the leader of that defense — one that was pretty good until the whole team became a dumpster fire this season.

Aside from cap and roster, Henley also fits well into the Broncos' long-term plans through his coverage ability. This has been an annoyingly difficult area to address and this defense's biggest weaknesses in pass defense. Coming out of college, scouting reports noted his upside and his sideline-to-sideline speed. He was considered underweight and not a great tackler. However, in the NFL that slight weight hasn't stopped him from being the Chargers' leading tackler every season.

I think this trade is exactly what the defense needs to take things to an elite level. All that remains to be seen is how well he fits into the Vance Joseph scheme this year.

#2798. Millions of dollars poured into prediction markets on election night, trading on Democratic control of Congress and Texas governor's race

More than 87% of all election markets across Kalshi and Polymarket gave the right candidate at least a 90% chance of winning their race 24 hours before election night, a CNBC analysis found.

Election night showed how traders reacted to real-time midterm results, as trading activity surged and market prices shifted to Democrats after results from Indiana began rolling in before 7 p.m. on Nov. 3. Many midterm races were uncompetitive, which boosted the overall hit rate on prediction markets.

"I'd say prediction markets did pretty well," said Koleman Strumpf, a professor of economics at Wake Forest University. "But they didn't outperform the best," he added, referring to traditional forecast polls that tracked results that night.

Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls.

Prediction markets saw big trades on election night.

After 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, at least $1 million was traded on a Kalshi market that incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott would be reelected. Abbott eventually lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa by more than 700,000 votes, according to the Associated Press. A little after 11 p.m. on election night, more than $1.4 million was traded on Kalshi that Republicans would not secure control of the House of Representatives.

Following the midterms, both Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan and Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour were on the social media platform X crediting prediction markets for correctly predicting races. Nate Silver, a political forecaster and founder of the Silver Bulletin newsletter, disputed the claim, arguing forecast models influenced prediction market movement. Silver joined Polymarket as an advisor in 2024.

"Prediction market probabilities strongly converged toward [our models] in individual Senate and gubernatorial races," Silver wrote on Silver Bulletin. "I was tracking this stuff closely, precisely because I envisioned that we might wind up in this sort of debate where prediction markets are low-key stealing valor from the models."

Prediction market volume on midterm election-related contracts across Kalshi and Polymarket more than tripled from the last week of October into the midterms week, according to a CNBC analysis of data published on Prediction.com. The data did not include combo markets, which bundle multiple contracts and pay out only if every leg resolves in the trader's favor.

Still, volume on midterm contracts pales in comparison with sports volume, which remains larger than all other categories.

Kalshi exceeded $3 billion in total midterm contract volume, according to the platform's website, which also includes volume for contracts on mayoral races. Last week, Polymarket's two exchanges reported nearly $700 million in volume for midterm contracts.

While prediction markets broadly anticipated Democratic control of Congress, the blue tsunami is expected to bite the industry in other ways.

Three days after the midterms, Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif, criticized the federal regulator responsible for the platforms, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, for allowing sports contracts.

"Sports prediction markets are sports bets. By effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states, even on Tribal lands, the CFTC is once again violating state law and Tribal sovereignty," Schiff wrote on X.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

Draymond Green states potential Jordan Poole-Warriors reunion a 'non-issue' originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Three seasons and 11 games have passed since Jordan Poole has played for the Warriors.

Despite the ugly conflict with Draymond Green that precipitated his exit, Poole said after the Warriors' win Monday over his New Orleans Pelicans that he would consider returning "home" to the team that drafted him in 2019.

Considering the nature of that incident, it would be fair to ask if Green would have an issue playing alongside Poole again.

"I have no issue with that at all," Green said in the locker room after the game, according to Bay Area News Group's Joseph Dycus. "I will never stand in the way of this organization thinking they can better themselves."

Seeing those last two quoted sentences in social media posts, many fans speculated that Green was inferring Poole would be the one to have an issue with a reunion.

Green, on his podcast "The Draymond Green Show," clarified his postgame comments, pointing out that any decision regarding a Poole-Warriors reunion comes down to the organizations, and not himself.

"What those comments were — they asked me about Jordan Poole's comments … and they were asking me, like, how did I feel about that," Green recalled on his podcast. "And I told them I don't have a problem with that at all. Number one, I don't make decisions here. I'm a basketball player. I don't decide my own future here, let alone someone else's …

"Number two, what I said was also, I'm an adult. So if you're asking me as if that's going to be a problem for me, that's no problem for me … I'm not someone who walks around with a grudge."

The San Francisco Standard's Danny Emerman provided another quote from Green from Monday night, in which the Warriors veteran further explained how he has moved on from the incident, and that the decision around Poole returning does not fall on him.

"We had our issue that I f–ked up on, and that's that," Green said, according to Emerman. "But I'm not one to hold grudges, I'm not one to sit around and try to damper something for someone else. So if that's what he wants, I understand that.

"But that's not a Draymond issue. That's a Golden State Warriors decision."

In his podcast, Green provided an example of a similar situation, saying that Warriors general manager Mike Dunleavy asked him about his thoughts on trading for then-Washington Wizards guard Chris Paul. Green recalled that he told his GM that the two did not see "eye-to-eye" and that he couldn't say that he was "very fond of him at all."

"I told Mike then — I said, 'Mike, I wouldn't stand in the way of what you think this team needs, or what can help make this team better,'" Green recalled telling Dunleavy. "I would never stand in the way of that. And so, same went for last night when I was asked that …

"… If they were like, 'Man, we're bringing Jordan Poole in' — whether that's a trade, whatever it is — and I was still [with the Warriors], that's a non-issue for me."

Green seems to be abstinent when it comes to personnel decisions at this point in his career, and that extends to any possible reunion with Poole.

#2795. A massive trade in Nvidia just went off – here are the details

The biggest options trade on Nvidia stock Monday seems to think the controversy swirling around the chip leader and its embattled CEO is creating a buying opportunity.In a trade about an hour after the opening bell that involved more than $100 million in options premium, someone exchanged an existing call spread for a more bullish position that captures the next five months of trading in Nvidia.The core position was the purchase of 52,000 195-strike calls expiring Feb. 19 worth about $57 million – contracts the trader opened for a new long position while simultaneously selling the same number of 245-strike calls for the same expiry, lowering the cost of the trade by $10 million. The net position, a bullish call spread, needs Nvidia to trade above around $206 by expiry, or about 15% higher, to be profitable. If Nvidia stock reaches the short, 245-strike call, it would represent a nearly 40% rally and return the stock to its all-time high of $243, that was reached on October 6th.The trade was likely part of a "roll" down from an existing 210/255-strike call spread worth about $42 million that was closed out, according to SpotGamma analysis.

"The person got more aggressive rolling this spread down to lower strikes to get more upside exposure by getting higher delta," SpotGamma founder Brent Kochuba said by phone. "They're trading the call spread here because the vol is expensive going into earnings. It's a significant increase in upside delta exposure."Delta is options parlance for describing how quickly an options price will react to a change in the underlying stock price. The trader's updated position, taken at lower strikes, will make money faster if Nvidia rallies. In other words, it's a higher conviction trade that the chipmaker's stock will soon rebound. The 195-strike calls they bought for $57 million was the single biggest options trade on the tape Monday, according to SpotGamma. Of the top 20 options trades by dollar-amount, 12 were Nvidia, the data show.Flows around the stock generally leaned bullish by midday, with 57% of options volume tied to calls and more than $660 million of call premium likely initiated by call-buyers, SpotGamma data show. The most popular single contract by volume was the 180-strike call expiring Monday, that needs Nvidia to recover 1.2% by the bell to break even.

Keenan was a seventh-round draft pick of the Los Angeles Rams this year out of Alabama. He was waived in September. The Raiders then signed him to their practice squad.

Keenan played in all three games he was elevated for and he even started in Week 9 at San Francisco, playing a season high 49 percent of the snaps. He has played in 35 percent of the snaps in his three games. He has a total of seven tackles with four coming against the 49ers.

Expect him to continue to be part of the playing rotation for the rest of the season.

To replace Keenan on the practice squad, the Raiders signed defensive tackle Chris Williams. He has been in the NFL since 2020 and was part of the Falcons' and Browns' programs this year.

#2792. Former Ohio State star has one word to describe the Buckeyes loss

Ohio State's blowout loss to Oregon has drawn plenty of criticism from Buckeyes fans and former players alike. And two of the program's former stars are among the most frustrated.

Former Ohio State running back Beanie Wells called the loss "embarrassing," taking particular aim at the Buckeyes' defense, as national champion quarterback Cardale Jones agreed with that assessment.

Ohio State jumped out to a 14-0 lead against Oregon on Saturday, but the Ducks scored 38 straight points on their way to a 41-28 win. It was the Buckeyes' second straight loss after falling 30-18 at USC, and it was their first time losing back-to-back games to unranked opponents since 1992.

Former Buckeyes blasted the team after the game, and Barstool's Brandon Walker said that Ryan Day is "doing the worst job of his entire career." Ohio State then fired Discher just nine games into his first season, and Day said this week that Luke Fahey will remain the starter against Northwestern.

When host Dave Holmes of The Script podcast asked the pair of former Buckeyes for their reactions to Ohio State's loss this week, Wells didn't hold back.

"Oh, it's wild. And, you know, I use the word a little bit loosely at times, but this is, you know, very much indeed what it is: embarrassing," Wells said on The Script. "When you look at the performances that we've had in these big matchups, when you look at the inability to be able to get to the passer, be able to stop plays on third down, and more importantly, just be able to stop explosive gains. I mean, that's not Ohio State football."

"When we talk about Ohio State defenses, we typically talk about the Silver Bullets. Well, there's no bullets flying. I think we all are out of bullets at this point in time," Wells continued.

Jones argued that Ohio State's defensive numbers were inflated by weak competition, and that the Buckeyes keep coming up short against good teams.

"We were stacking up against those top defenses because we was going against really bad offenses," Jones said. "We continue to fall short in these big matchups of recently. So that is an issue of concern."

Needless to say, some of the program's former players are just as frustrated as the fans.
