#2789. 2026 NFL Trade Deadline Fantasy Fallout: Colts keep Jonathan Taylor, Chiefs deal for Josh Downs, 49ers land Keenan Allen

The NFL trade deadline is complete and fantasy football is in a whirlwind! Fantasy analyst Joel Smyth breaks down some key deals. And go here for Hayden Winks' breakdown of Kirk Cousins' return to Minnesota.

This trade is not only a win but a lifesaver for Josh Downs' fantasy outlook (you can read the full trade terms here). He's the dynasty fantasy winner of the day if he re-signs with the Chiefs, and he can finally be usable in redraft leagues!

The Colts lost Alec Pierce to injury and traded Michael Pittman Jr., yet Downs was still limited to a sub-20% target share. Kansas City has a similar lack of pass-catchers as Indianapolis, but gives Downs more of a chance as one of the most talented receivers in a new offense. He should fit well on a team that has the lowest average depth of target in the NFL.

I'm worried for Rice once Downs is playing full snaps, but researching helped ease concerns a little bit. The negatives: Rice is a volume-dependent WR. He had been recently looking much improved compared to the first few weeks of the season. However, his style is very similar to Downs', running over 50% of routes from the slot, and having over 70% of receiving fantasy points coming on throws under 10 air yards. The big positive here is the schedule, not in terms of fantasy points allowed to WRs, but the game scripts ahead. In a five-game stretch, the Chiefs play the Bills, Rams, Bengals, Patriots and 49ers, all teams that can bump up the passing volume and scoring. Surprisingly, the Chiefs rank third in pass rate over expected, behind only the Packers and Bengals; they have just been consistently in the lead.

The Chiefs' upcoming schedule might be more impactful for Mahomes than Downs, although the deal is a positive. The passing production for Mahomes over the past few years has been modest in fantasy, often relying on his rushing for his ceiling, and I'm not sure this massively changes anything. It's a plus, but maybe a 1-PPG bump compared to having a different wideout in the game.

Jonathan Taylor is the lone survivor in Indianapolis. After dealing Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Keenan Allen (more on him below) and Josh Downs, the Colts decided to hold on to Taylor in a failing season without their first-round draft pick available. The share of touches that has dipped down to 63% in the last few weeks should rise back up for Taylor, as there is less reason to save his legs. The only other positives are the schedule should keep some games close, and the receiving, which has often been underrated for Taylor, should be solid overall. However, the negatives win outright, with Taylor's ceiling coming when the touchdowns pile up. Since Week 5, the Colts offense ranks 31st in touchdowns per game with 1.4. He's still startable in fantasy, but the long-term risk is elevated.

Allen has quietly put together a solid fantasy season, outscoring Downs with 10.1 PPR PPG while inside the top 20 WRs in targets. The targets should still be available in San Francisco (go here for the full trade details), with no WR having over a 10% target share outside of Mike Evans. The 49ers have been fantasy gold for receivers this decade, often overlooked because of the lack of one sticking long term. Since 2020, they rank first in fantasy points per target and still second in 2026 to the Cincinnati Bengals.

Especially when other wideouts are not available, Allen can continue to be played as a flex option, now more confidently.

#2788. Winderman’s view: Desperate times? Spoelstra shows in Heat win he’s not waiting

Observations and other notes of interest from Tuesday night's 115-109 victory over the Utah Jazz:

– Giannis Antetokounmpo was questionable 90 minutes before tip-off. He played.

– Andrew Wiggins was reduced to a reserve role for the second time in as many games.

– Myron Gardner and Simone Fontecchio played in the second quarter while Tim Hardaway Jr. remained planted on the bench.

– OK, perhaps not desperate measures, but also no time to fool around.

– Such is the reality of battling back from an 0-4 start to the season.

– Erik Spoelstra could not have sent more specific messages to end the five-game trip.

– Play well, do the right things . . . or don't play.

– Even with a somewhat shaky finish to this one.

– Winning three out of four against the Clippers, Kings and Jazz isn't necessarily something.

– But based on the way the Heat started the season, it also isn't nothing.

– The theme from Spoelstra amid this climb back from the 0-4 start has been small, subtle steps.

– "I see some things trending in a better direction," he said. "And these little mini victories that you have an opportunity for, you want to seize those opportunities."

– For the second consecutive game, the Heat opened with a lineup of Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo, Klay Thompson, Davion Mitchell and Pelle Larsson.

– For the first time this season, Keshad Johnson was active for the Heat on his two-way contract.

– Tre Donaldson and Vlad Goldin again were inactive on their two-way deals.

– The very-shorthanded Jazz opened with a lineup of Darryn Peterson , Josh Green , Josh Okogie, Ace Bailey and Jaxson Hayes.

– Among those sidelined for the Jazz were Keyonte George, Jaren Jackson Jr., Lauri Markkanen and Jusuf Nurkic.

– So basically four of their five starters and four of their six-best players.

– With Utah short on big bodies, Jazz coach Will Hardy spoke pregame of the challenge ahead.

– "For years with Giannis, the point of contact is always so important because you can keep the ball in front but drop too far back," he said. "Bam also commands a lot of respect in terms of we need to show multiple bodies. So it's going to be like every night. It's a team defense night. Recognizing some of the size differential in different matchups, we're going to need to show those secondary bodies a little bit earlier."

– It helped the Jazz that Antetokounmpo got into early foul trouble.

– Ryan Conwell again got early action off the Heat bench, entering along with Bobby Portis Jr. in the Heat's first substitution, midway through the opening period.

– Wiggins followed third off the Heat bench shortly thereafter.

– And then the rotation got even more unconventional, with Gardner and Fontecchio entering at the start of the second period, as Hardaway remained planted on the bench.

– Wiggins' second 3-pointer was the 1,300th of his career.

– Of the evolution of his team's second unit, Spoelstra said, "It can be a chaos lineup, defensive swarm, and get some easy ones in transition. We'll get that sorted through."

– Of Hardaway attempting to find his way back amid limited minutes, Spoelstra said, "I understand it, and it is tough. Some of these decisions are tough for me. It's tough for some of the guys to find their rhythm."

– Spoelstra added, "Be a positive on the scoreboard, change the energy of the game, and then we'll sort through rhythm, touches, getting guys playing comfortable."

– During the opening period, the Jazz lost a challenge and even more.

– The Jazz challenged a charging foul drawn by Mitchell. Upon review, referee Scott Foster said the ball was deflected before the block/charge contact.

– So instead of the original charge call on the Jazz and Heat possession, the Heat were awarded two free throws on the loose-ball foul.

– Shades of Dick Bavetta. So Jazz challenge . . . gives Heat two free throws.

– Spoelstra said among the goals in getting the defense back on track is a team-wide commitment against the pick-and-roll.

– "The mentality and mindset is five guys attacking the pick-and-roll," he said. "It has to be that. It can't just be the two players involved in the pick-and-roll, because there's going to be a lot of other weak side things that happen from that."

– On that theme, Adebayo said of the pick-and-roll defense, "For us, it's getting our coverages right, making the right calls and believing that we can get deflections and steals."

– Of opponents loading up on 3-pointers this season against the Heat, Adebayo said it's a whole new world in that regard,

– "I mean guys, we've seen it from 30 feet," he said of a distance nearly seven-feet beyond the arc. "So it's a longer closeout game than it was four or five years ago. So for us, it's understanding that there are longer closeouts and understanding that we've got to get out there."

– Going in, the Heat's numbers with Adebayo on the floor and Antetokounmpo off were actually better offensively than defensively, which assuredly would not have been expected.

#2785. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2784. The Kirk Cousins contract points to a revised deal or termination after 2026

The last time the Vikings brought back a key former player for a third-round pick, the reunion didn’t last long. This time, it will last longer — but possibly not beyond the current season.

In 2010, the Vikings sent a third-round pick to the Patriots for receiver Randy Moss, whom the Vikings had traded to the Raiders in 2005. Former coach Brad Childress, calling Moss a “programmatic non-fit,” released Moss after four games.

Now, quarterback Kirk Cousins returns for a third-round pick, and a contract that covers nine regular-season games. His deal with the Raiders was structured to maximize the amount the Falcons owed Cousins for 2026 ($8.7 million, on top of the $90 million he made in 2024 and 2025) with another $10 million paid by the Raiders to Cousins in 2027, in the form of a guaranteed roster bonus not subject to offset.

The contract also includes a 2028 base salary of $78.655 million that becomes fully guaranteed on the fifth day of the 2027 league year. Coupled with a $1.345 million base salary in 2027 that becomes fully guaranteed that same day, the Vikings would be on the hook for $80 million over two years if he’s not released by then.

Without a revised deal, the current contract surely would be torn up by March. The question is whether the Vikings and Cousins would be able to come up with a new contract to replace it.

Much of that depends on how the rest of the year goes. Still, Cousins has the ability to force his way to free agency, for the fourth time in his career, by simply declining to re-do the existing deal.

However it plays out, Cousins can be counted on to make a good business decision. He has $333 million in career earnings, which has him at fourth on the all-time list.

On-field success is a different story. He has made it to the postseason three times in his career, with one playoff win.

If, as expected, the return of Cousins provides a B-12 shot to the Minnesota franchise, he has a realistic chance of getting back to the playoffs. And of winning a second postseason game.

And maybe a third. Hell, maybe even a fourth.

#2783. Heat end trip with shaky victory over shorthanded Jazz behind Giannis’ 30 and 11

SALT LAKE CITY – Against another opponent on another night, the Miami Heat's momentum might have stalled. Instead the perfect opponent to end a five-game, 10-day trip.

Against a team that entered 1-9 and was without four of five starters, the Heat made it three victories in their last four games with a 115-109 victory Tuesday night over the Utah Jazz at Delta Center.

While it wasn't as easy as expected, and while the record still is underwater at 5-6, the victory completed a 3-2 western swing for Erik Spoelstra's team, with a five-game homestand to follow.

Not only did the Jazz enter with the league's worst record, but they were without starters Keyonte George, Jaren Jackson Jr., Lauri Markkanen and Jusuf Nurkic.

So while it was somewhat shaky, the Heat did (barely) enough, even with Giannis Antetokounmpo battling an ongoing wrist issue and this time foul trouble, as well.

With Antetokounmpo still working his way to 30 points and 11 rebounds, the Heat had enough against an opponent that got 25 points from No. 2 2026 draft pick Darryn Peterson and 23 from Ace Baily.

In support of Antetokounmpo, the Heat got 19 points, eight assists and five rebounds from Davion Mitchell, on a night Bam Adebayo was held to 11 points along with eight rebounds.

Five Degrees of Heat from Tuesday night's game:

1. Game flow: The Heat led 29-25 after the first period. They then pushed their lead to 17 in the second period, and then went into halftime up 64-54, unable to build more of a lead despite 11 first-half Jazz turnovers.

The Jazz then trimmed their deficit to six early in the third period, before the Heat pushed their lead to 85-66 on an Antetokounmpo 3-pointer midway through the third, going up 23, before taking a 92-72 into the fourth.

From there, though, the Jazz moved within 101-93 with 6:42 to play on consecutive Isaiah Collier 3-pointers.

That is when Antetokounmpo settled the offense, as the Heat mostly settled the game, aided by a Klay Thompson chase-down block when the Jazz threatened to close within five with 65 seconds to play.

And even then, it required another transition block, this time by Adebayo, when the Jazz threatened to close within three with 22.1 seconds to play.

Antetokounmpo closed 12 of 21 from the field, 5 of 9 from the line, with free throws remaining an ongoing Heat issue.

Coffee connoisseur. Domino don. Coach Jimmy?

Jimmy Butler has no shortage of hobbies and side gigs to keep him busy even while unable to get on the court for the Warriors while rehabbing the ACL he tore in January. He added another Monday night, to the amusement of his Golden State teammates.

At least one of them would prefer to see Butler stick to his dayjob(s), though.

"Man, nah, nah, nah. He gotta go home," Warriors guard De'Anthony Melton told the NBC Sports Bay Area broadcast following the 138-87 win over the Pelicans. "The next time he do something like that, he gotta go back home or do something else. Because he trippin'."

De'Anthony Melton of the Golden State Warriors speaks to the media after a game against the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in San Francisco. NBAE via Getty Images

Melton was on the receiving end of Butler's most pointed coaching advice of the night.

Taking his usual seat on the bench, Butler traded in his typically fashion-forward wardrobe for a white pullover and black joggers — the same get-up as Steve Kerr and the rest of the Warriors coaching staff. He also grabbed a clipboard, which came in handy to remind Melton of the golden rule of basketball in Golden State: Pass the ball to Steph Curry.

When Melton checked out midway through the third quarter, Butler spelled it out loud and clear in blue ink on the clipboard and held it up for Melton — and the cameras — to see.

Georges Niang, left, and Jimmy Butler III smile after a game at Chase Center in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Melton had just violated the one and only edict on two possessions in quick succession. Curry was open on the perimeter but Melton drove to the rim through traffic and failed to convert.

Butler offered him — and the rest of the Warriors — a simple reminder.

"All I learned is once you're on the court with Steph, give Steph the ball," rookie Yaxel Lendeborg said of Butler as a tactician. "Just get the ball to Steph. That's the most serious thing he said."

Stephen Curry (30) of the Golden State Warriors prepares to shoot against the New Orleans Pelicans on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in San Francisco. Getty Images

Butler gave his teammates no advance notice of his plans for the game. Lendeborg even mistook him for a regular member of the coaching staff at first.

Butler's wardrobe ensured that he would blend right in on the bench.

"I thought he looked great. Really good-looking sweater," Kerr quipped. "He said all the right things. Team fouls. How many team fouls we had. He was really acting the part. But I also realized he was mocking us, so it hurt a little bit."

It was all in good fun, but Melton agreed: he preferred Butler on the court than the bench.

"No. Just no," Melton said with a laugh when asked about Butler's coaching debut. "I think he just got fired today, which is actually crazy. I'm happy about that."

#2780. CoreWeave earnings put debt-fueled AI build-out under scrutiny

CoreWeave faces a pivotal test when it reports its third-quarter financial results after the bell on Tuesday.

The market will be closely watching what the neocloud company says about artificial intelligence spending — and how it plans to finance its infrastructure buildout. The outcome could either calm concerns over its debt or stoke more fear.

"Investors need neoclouds to quantify how much financing they expect to raise to execute on existing backlog," Wolfe Research said in a note Monday. "We think outlooks that communicate when and which avenues of funding will be tapped will increase investor confidence."

CoreWeave stock and bonds have come under pressure as fears deepened about the enormous amount of debt it has taken out to build its data centers.

Its stock is down roughly 40% over the past month. Meanwhile, the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 15.5% on Tuesday, after jumping to 16.7% on Thursday as investors digested the election results and possible roadblocks to data center construction. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

The spread on its five-year credit default swaps — which is insurance against default and considered a barometer of perceived credit risk — is also at levels that are considered distressed. On Tuesday, its CDS spread stood around 1,152 basis points, after rising above its October peak to close at 1,278 basis points on Thursday. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

In addition, the New Jersey-based company's leverage is high. CoreWeave has a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from almost 291% a year ago.

CEO Michael Intrator has sought to quell investor fear, posting on LinkedIn after the election last week that the company doesn't anticipate "any impact to CoreWeave's existing customer commitments or associated backlog as a result of shifts in the political landscape."

The company reported a revenue backlog of $104.2 billion in the second quarter. It has about $35 billion in debt, as of June 30.

CoreWeave has already given a picture of what it expects for the third quarter.

It guided for quarterly revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion when it reported second-quarter results in August. It anticipated capital expenditures between $11.5 billion and $13.5 billion for the quarter and $35 billion to $39 billion for the full year. The company also expects 1.85 gigawatts in active power by year-end.

Wells Fargo expects the company's capex needs for the rest of the year to be largely covered by its remaining undrawn debt, debt issuances in August/September and the $12 billion it is holding for project costs, which will flow into capex, analyst Michael Turrin said in a note Sunday.

However, its 2027 capex could reach $66 billion, based on an expected capacity addition of 1.5 gigawatts, Turrin said. That will require at least $25 billion more in debt, he noted. It can be largely funded through delayed draw term loans, which allows CoreWeave to draw down funds over time, and the rest can come through bonds and convertibles, he said.

Turrin has an overweight rating and $115 price target on the stock, implying 135% upside from Monday's close.

"While neoclouds sit in the eye of the AI storm, we remain confident that CRWV is the highest quality co in the space," Turrin wrote. "Beyond the noise, we see capacity/revs coming in better than expected (1.95GW this yr vs guide 1.85GW) as margins start to inflect."

However, investors likely won't get all the answers they're seeking during CoreWeave's third-quarter results, said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin.

"One of the major issues for CoreWeave is whether or not they can obtain all the financing they need," he said. "They may try and calm the markets, but I'm not sure how much color they can and will provide."

Investors will be looking for 2027 guidance on capex and free cash flow, though that may not come until Coreweave releases fourth quarter results, Chalfin notes.

CoreWeave could ease investor concerns by showing it has plans and approvals in place to scale capacity through 2027, he said. The company can also demonstrate remaining performance obligation (RPO) growth, which shows the total value of its contracted future revenue, and highlight new customer wins.

In addition, pricing has been really strong on recent deals, Chalfin pointed out. "That could show up in an operating margin beat for Q3 and expectations for Q4."

While CoreWeave faces finances challenges, the company has many ways to access capital, Chalfin said. That includes chip-backed deals, which allow Corewave to borrow money using GPUs as collateral, and original equipment manufacturer financing. For instance, CoreWeave could turn to Dell, which is a big supplier with a strong balance sheet, Chalfin noted.

"Despite all the market sentiment, fundamentals are actually quite strong and pricing is strong," he said. "The trends over the next few quarters, I think, should be supportive." Risks could arise after that, but it is "too early to call."

Some analysts remain skeptical that Coreweave will be able to calm credit fears.

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, points out that the company is facing a huge bill in just over two years. CoreWeave owes roughly $15 billion in principal payments through 2028, according to its second-quarter earnings statement.

"They don't have enough cash to service all that debt," he said. "Unless some big orders come in, unless some big money flows come in for them in the next 17, 18 months, I think this is going to be the start of the end for CoreWeave, unless somebody comes in and wants to buy them. But who wants to buy all that debt?"

However, there could be a "small" window for the company to push out its debt for another three to five years, but it will depend on how strong their cash flow is when they report on Tuesday, Lang said.

Plus, issuing equity to help fund infrastructure projects, like Meta and Oracle did recently, isn't an option for CoreWeave, he noted.

"They're going to dilute the stock so much that it's going to continue to go down," he said. "They missed that window when the stock was in the hundreds."

CoreWeave topped $183 in June 2025. It has since declined more than 73%, recently trading around $47.

Despite the fall, analysts remain bullish on the stock with an average overweight rating and $126 target, based on 39 estimates complied by FactSet.

—CNBC's Jordan Novet contributed reporting.

#2775. JJ Redick feels Lakers wins over Pistons, Hawks were ‘great examples’ of next guy up

Despite missing Luka Dončić Sunday against the Detroit Pistons and Austin Reaves Monday against the Atlanta Hawks, the Los Angeles Lakers went on the road for a back-to-back set and won both games over two of the Eastern Conference's top-four seeds.

On Sunday, Reaves' 43 points led the Lakers while Dončić's 32-point, 10-assist double-double paced them Monday night. But in both outings, Los Angeles' depth played crucial roles to fill the void vacated by the absence of a star guard. Sandro Mamukelashvili, Collin Sexton and Ziaire Williams all delivered, helping propel Los Angeles to a pair of impressive road victories — and head coach JJ Redick recognized their efforts.

"I think the last two games, great examples of next guy up," Redick told reporters postgame Monday. "…I thought Collin did a really nice job of attacking the paint and scoring. Giving us some juice, especially there in the first half. Sandro, his best game as a Laker and whatever he had, 23 points. That was awesome. Made some big time plays. I thought the two defensive rebounds he got there in the last few minutes were as big as any play he made all night."

Walker Kessler filled up the stat sheet across both games, averaging 16.5 points, 13 rebounds, 4.0 assists, 2.0 blocks and 1.0 steals to fortify the interior on both ends. His rebounding, finishing, rim protection and quick decision-making are integral to Los Angeles' 10-2 start this season.

Of course, Dončić and Reaves will shepherd the Lakers' success — as they have through three weeks — but the supporting cast members elevating their play when called upon will be necessary if the Lakers are to contend for a title.

"It's building resiliency. JJ talks about it, going through adversity, and understanding that, to be a championship team, you've got to respond to that kind of stuff," Kessler said Monday. "When they made their fourth quarter run, we responded accordingly and got the win."

Los Angeles will look to extend its winning streak to seven games and maintain an undefeated road trip when it faces the Milwaukee Bucks Wednesday night. Tipoff is scheduled for 5 p.m. PST.

#2772. Paul George Outplays Jaylen Brown in First Battle of Celtics-76ers Trade Centerpieces

Paul George Outplays Jaylen Brown in First Battle of Celtics-76ers Trade Centerpieces originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Plenty of basketball fans were excited to watch the individual battle between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown on Tuesday, but another star forward stole the show.

Paul George scored a game-high 36 points on 14-of-22 shooting from the field in the Celtics' 123-101 win over the 76ers, helping his team jump to the top of the Eastern Conference standings.

George, who landed in Boston as part of the offseason trade that sent Brown to Philadelphia, had 14 of his 36 points in the fourth quarter, and the Celtics outscored the Sixers 32-19 in the final frame.

"What I've learned is, I'm a little bit better with more usage," George said during an appearance on NBC's postgame show. "That's not a knock to my opportunities here in Philly. Quite frankly, I wasn't healthy [enough] to take on the workload.

"Here in Boston, they gave me an opportunity to come out and play and be myself. Joe [Mazzulla] has integrated me right into the offense and allowed me to just be myself."

That performance continued an impressive start for George, who noted that his body is "holding up wonderfully" after dealing with multiple injuries in his two seasons with the 76ers. Heading into the rivalry matchup, he was averaging 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals per game while shooting 42.5 percent from 3-point range.

"The beauty of this offense is the game is just gonna find me," George said. "That's one thing Joe preaches within our offense, just let it find you. I'm not pressing. I'm not rushing. I'm not forcing. I've always played that game, and my best nights have come from me just letting the game happen. That's when I'm at my best."

Brown, on the other hand, had a night to forget. He wasn't able to get revenge against his former squad, scoring just 13 points in 26 minutes. Foul trouble limited his impact, as he picked up two fouls in the first quarter.

"Just got those two early fouls that kind of distorted my rhythm throughout the whole game and kind of struggled to get it back," Brown said (via The Philadelphia Inquirer's Chris Hine). "We had opportunities to get back into the game. It was a tie game at one point. They shot the hell out of the ball, executed well. We gotta get better."

The 2024 Finals MVP finished with a plus-minus of minus-27, the worst mark of any player on either team. George had a plus-minus of plus-17.

Of course, it's a little early to declare that Celtics president of basketball operations Brad Stevens has already been vindicated for his bold move. For one night, though, George showed exactly why Boston was willing to pull the trigger on such a controversial deal.

#2769. Raiders rookie QB Fernando Mendoza will make first career start vs. Seahawks after Kirk Cousins trade: 'He's prepared'

Fernando Mendoza, a reigning college national champion, will face the defending Super Bowl champions in his first career NFL start.

Mendoza, who led Indiana on a storybook run to College Football Playoff glory, will get the nod for the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium against the Seattle Seahawks, general manager John Spytek and head coach Klint Kubiak confirmed Tuesday.

Mendoza, the No. 1 overall draft pick in April, is up for a 4-5 Raiders team that traded veteran Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings for a 2027 third-round pick hours before Tuesday's trade deadline. That deal effectively marked the beginning of the Mendoza era in Vegas.

"This is something that he's worked very hard for since the moment he walked into this building," said Spytek, who emphasized in a news conference alongside Kubiak that the Cousins trade doesn't mean the Raiders are punting on the season or looking ahead to 2027.

Spytek added, regarding Mendoza: "He passed every test. I want to stop short of saying he's earned it, but he put us in a position where we had to make a really hard decision today with his growth as a person, as a teammate, as a leader, as a quarterback."

After learning under the 38-year-old Cousins before and during the season, the 23-year-old Mendoza is set for quite the three-game test in advance of the Raiders' Week 13 bye.

Not only will he have to battle the Seahawks' vaunted defense, but he'll have to go up against the Denver Broncos and Cleveland Browns the subsequent two weeks. Entering Week 10, all three of those teams rank inside the top 13 in fewest points per game allowed this season. The Broncos and Browns are tied with a handful of teams for fourth in the NFL with 26 sacks.

Mendoza has attempted only eight regular-season passes. All of those came in relief of Cousins down the stretch of a 45-17 road loss to the New England Patriots. That was part of a four-game Raiders skid that followed their head-turning 3-0 start.

In his first year at the helm, Kubiak named Cousins the team's Week 1 starter after evaluating both him and Mendoza in the preseason. He then stuck with Cousins under center despite the October losing streak.

Cousins was open throughout his stay in Las Vegas that he was well aware of the circumstances of his role and that his time as Raiders QB1 was limited. He stressed that he wanted to put the team in the best position to win games, even if that meant at some point handing the baton to Mendoza.

But Cousins played so well that he kept his job leading up to the deadline. In fact, an ESPN report surfaced Sunday morning, detailing how, at the time, the Raiders weren't interested in dealing him.

Spytek explained Tuesday that the trade really came together with the Vikings that morning.

"I never made one call on Kirk Cousins," Spytek said, when asked if the Raiders were shopping Cousins. "I got a few phone calls, but one real one this morning."

Both Spytek and Kubiak were effusive about Cousins in the fallout of the trade. Spytek even divulged that, before Las Vegas made the final call on dealing Cousins, he and Kubiak sat with the longtime signal-caller to talk him through the deal.

"We both felt like it was important that he have say in it, too," Spytek said. "Fifteen-year veteran, everything he's given to this organization, he has a family and we kind of presented him with what we had on the table, and we tried to make the best decision. I think we owed him that respect."

Kubiak noted: "It reinforced how extremely unselfish he is and just the way that he spoke to us and the maturity and the awareness of the situation — I think we all left that room on the same page, all with respect for one another."

Kirk Cousins (right) willingly adopted a mentor role with the Raiders, assisting Fernando Mendoza (left) in his development as an NFL quarterback.

Cousins turned back the clock while working with Kubiak, posting a 20:8 touchdown-to-interception ratio. His 20 TD passes are good for second most in the league and already more than he's had in a season since his 2022 campaign with the Vikings, with whom he played from 2018-2023.

Cousins turned out to be among the best NFL rentals in recent memory. The Raiders paid him a total of $650,000, per ESPN's Field Yates, and his value resulted in a third-round pick and priceless mentorship.

He appeared to forge an endearing friendship with Mendoza, who eagerly absorbed tips and tricks from Cousins.

Kubiak said Tuesday that Cousins' influence "will remain on our team throughout this season."

He added: "And it remains with Fernando."

Kubiak was asked directly Tuesday if he feels like it helped Mendoza that he wasn't thrown in from Day 1.

"I do," Kubiak said with a soft smile. "Yes, I do. I think with the right role model, that will accelerate his growth, and we had the right role model."

Las Vegas drafted Mendoza first overall in the aftermath of his prolific 2025 season with the Hoosiers. He won the Heisman Trophy, vaulted himself into the end zone en route to beating Miami in the national title game and finished the season with 48 total touchdowns, including 41 through the air.

His effervescence, often on full display in postgame interviews, made him a unique college football star. He's still that happy-go-lucky QB, at least outside the white lines.

Time will tell how Mendoza's game translates to NFL regular-season play. He completed 6 of 8 passes against the Patriots for 48 yards. In the preseason, he had mixed results, impressing in his debut against the Arizona Cardinals and then throwing a pick-6 versus the Houston Texans and another interception against the San Francisco 49ers.

Mendoza wrapped the preseason with 240 yards on 25-of-45 passing, registering a 55.6% completion rate, one touchdown pass and those two picks.

It's been months since then, however. The Cousins trade speaks to Minnesota's desperation for a quarterback solution, but it also says a lot about the Raiders' trust in Mendoza's development.

"He's prepared, he's practiced extremely well," Kubiak said, "and his work habits also allow us to make this trade because we feel that he's ready to go, and we're excited to have him take the ball for the game here on Sunday."

Kubiak also said: "We knew this day was coming. We didn't know when it was going to be, but he's continued to grow since he's been here."

#2759. Breaking Down the Kings’ Decision to Move on from Nique Clifford

The Sacramento Kings' decision to part ways with Nique Clifford could confuse fans, especially given what they sacrificed to land him. Clifford came into the fold with high hopes as a young building block for the franchise, but it didn't work out as planned. Even though last season was his rookie campaign, Clifford failed to capitalize on the chances he was given and became an afterthought in the rotation. The Kings parted ways with Clifford for two second-round picks, and he is now on the way to OKC.

One of the major factors pushing Sacramento to cut ties with Clifford was his failure to establish himself in Doug Christie's rotation this season, despite the Kings' struggles. Although Clifford is only at the beginning of his professional basketball career, the team wanted to see improvement from a prospect who had shown promise in the past. Whether it was production, contribution, consistency, or being a solid asset when he had minutes on the court, he failed to show he would consistently bring anything useful to the squad.

One key factor indicating how much the team lost trust in Clifford is that other players were able to pass him in the rotation. To be more exact, both Daeqwon Plowden and Emmanuel Sharp became those players who got chances to play over Clifford. In addition, the emergence of Leaky Black became yet another player who moved ahead of Clifford in the Sacramento hierarchy. For a prospect expected to be among the team's younger core players, the news was hardly good.

Sacramento Kings guard Nique Clifford (10) shoots the ball against Los Angeles Clippers center Brook Lopez (11) during the third quarter at Intuit Dome. Photo Credit: Kiyoshi Mio, Imagn Images via Reuters Connect

Perhaps the hardest aspect of the entire scenario for Kings fans to deal with is Clifford's move to the Oklahoma City Thunder. The Thunder have proven themselves to be one of the best NBA franchises at nurturing young talent and finding players who fit its system. Clifford's ability to find his place on another team is therefore especially difficult for the people of Sacramento to digest. Nobody wants to see their former Kings prospect blossom into an NBA player after being traded by them.

Another reason Clifford's departure is hard to cope with is that Sacramento had to give up something substantial to draft him with the No. 24 pick in 2025. The Kings sent a 2027 first-round pick (top-16 pick via San Antonio) to Oklahoma City to land him. Future first-round picks are considered highly valuable assets, especially for an NBA team looking to build for the coming years. Fans naturally expect a longer period to evaluate such prospects and get better returns on the investment.

Overall, the Kings' decision has everything to do with striking a balance between patience and opportunity cost. While the Kings might be going through a rebuilding process, Sacramento definitely cannot afford to waste endless time on their young players as they sort themselves out. Rebuilding is about understanding who needs the chance and who doesn't belong there in the first place. Clifford only being in his second season makes this decision quite surprising, though.

But there's also the idea that the Kings have to build a culture of competitiveness rather than giving players minutes just because they're of age or draft-pick-heavy. Players are supposed to get a chance to prove themselves, but they have to show they can capitalize on that opportunity. Plowden, Sharp, and now Black have given the Kings additional options to consider, making it tougher for the team to pursue Clifford. Of course, letting go of a player drafted but holding on to him out of pure loyalty wouldn't necessarily help the team improve.

Without a doubt,  Clifford's departure from the Kings ranks as a huge letdown, considering all that was expected of him and what it cost the team to bring him to Sacramento. It became hard to keep him on the roster, given that he wasn't productive or couldn't hold a spot in the rotation.

The fact that Clifford was traded to OKC only frustrates fans further, who may wonder how he could have turned out differently in another setting. There is plenty of time for Clifford to grow into an excellent player, and the Thunder may yet make good use of his abilities.

#2752. Believe it, Lakers are NBA championship contenders

Luka Dončić is playing as though he's on a revenge tour and every opposing player has former Mavericks general manager Nico Harrison's face superimposed on it.

Austin Reaves is playing as though he were shortchanged by signing a four-year, $180 million deal over the summer, the richest contract in NBA history for a player who went undrafted.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic (77) shoots against Atlanta Hawks guard CJ McCollum during an NBA game, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

Walker Kessler is playing as though he's hellbent on fulfilling his vow to "run through a wall" for the Lakers after they emptied their treasure trove of draft capital to acquire him in July.

And the Lakers' role players are playing as though they deeply understood the assignment when they joined a 17-time championship franchise.

The Lakers have the league's best record at 10-2. They've won six games in a row.

That isn't a sentence we thought we'd write heading into this season. Not with nine new players. Not with so many question marks around their perimeter defense. Not with their lack of depth at backup center.

But now, Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka looks like the Albert Einstein of basketball rosters and coach JJ Redick looks like a superstar whisperer.

The Lakers last won a championship in 2020, their first title in 10 years.

They could snap their six-year drought this season.

Dončić is on a historic tear, averaging 39.3 points (49.8% shooting from the field, 40.7% from beyond the arc), 7.8 rebounds, 7.9 assists and two steals per game.

In his first nine games of the season, Dončić scored 361 points, surpassing Michael Jordan's 347 points in 1986-87 for the most points scored through that period in modern NBA history.

But what really made the Lakers look like contenders is how they played without Dončić (lower back tightness) on Sunday against the Pistons.

Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers reacts after a late second-half 3-point basket against the Detroit Pistons in Detroit, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Getty Images

Without the league's current front-runner for the MVP Award and against a Pistons team with the third-highest defensive rating, Reaves scored a season-high 43 points in the Lakers' 121-116 win.

He reminded everyone of what he can do when he's unleashed.

Reaves has quietly been putting together a spectacular season. He's averaging 25.3 points on a very efficient 50.8% from the field and 41.3% from beyond the arc.

He's the 15th leading scorer in the league, and of those ahead of him, only Giannis Antetokounmpo, Anthony Davis and Victor Wembanyama have higher field-goal percentages than Reaves.

And only Jamal Murray and Steph Curry are shooting at a higher percentage from beyond the 3-point line.

Dončić and Reaves are the NBA's highest-scoring duo by a mile, averaging 64.6 points, 12.6 more than the second-leading duo of Steph Curry and Yaxel Lendeborg, who are averaging a combined 52 points per game.

Then there's Kessler, who's averaging a double-double with 14.9 points and 10.8 rebounds per game.

When Reaves was out for Monday's 124-114 win over the Hawks because of an illness, Dončić got help from the Lakers' reserves, with Collin Sexton having an 18-point, six-assist performance and Sandro Mamukelashvili pouring in 23 points and grabbing eight rebounds.

Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler (14) shoots against Atlanta Hawks center Jock Landale (31) during an NBA basketball game, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Atlanta. AP Photo/Mike Stewart

The Lakers have the highest offensive rating in the league at 121.5. And even though they're 19th in defensive rating (113.8), they rank second in the league in steals per game (10.8), second in total deflections (240) and third in blocks per game (6.4).

Kessler leads the NBA in contested shots (140).

Heck, even Dončić, who has notoriously been slammed for his defense throughout his career, is showing a lot of effort on the less glamorous end of the court. He leads the league in defensive loose balls recovered (nine) and is tied for second in charges drawn (four).

Entering this season, it was presumed that the Lakers needed time to jell. It seemed as though they had major holes. They weren't ready to compete with the league's elite teams, such as the Thunder, Spurs or Knicks.

The Lakers have sprinted past their doubters, proving that they're a team to watch.

#2746. Collin Sexton has focused on patience as he tries to find role with Lakers

Over the past two games, Collin Sexton has been indispensable in powering the Los Angeles Lakers to wins with their star guards, Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves, each missing one contest.

Against the Detroit Pistons on Sunday, the veteran guard tallied 17 points (5-of-10 shooting), two assists and two rebounds. A day later, he followed that up with 18 points (6-of-11 shooting), six assists, two rebounds and one steal in Monday's win over the Atlanta Hawks.

If those consecutive performances are any indication, Sexton could be finding his footing after a slow start to 2026-27, which featured a calf strain that hampered him during training camp and preseason.

Through his first nine appearances, he averaged 8.7 points while shooting 40% from the floor and 25.8% from deep (49.5% true shooting). In this week's pair of victories, he's averaged 17.5 points on 52.4% shooting and 50% from deep (64.4% true shooting). Following those laudatory outings, Sexton said he feels he's inching closer to fully being himself again.

"I think maybe another week and a half, two weeks and I think I'll be back," he told reporters Monday. "Right now, these last two games felt really good. So I'm moving in the right direction."

As Sexton works to rediscover his rhythm, he's embracing patience.

"That's one word I've been using each and every day," he said. "I would say each and every day is going to have its ups, have its downs but I'm blessed to be healthy enough to go out."

Head coach JJ Redick is counting on Sexton to help steady second units for the Lakers, given he's their most talented scorer and qualified initiator off the bench. After Monday's win, he spoke about Sexton's role in keeping the offense humming when the speedy guard is at the forefront.

"I think the biggest thing [is] we're trying to get organized and and there's glimpses of really good organization when he's out there as the primary ball handler," Redick told reporters. "We got a little squirrely there at the end of the second quarter. #2741. Game Preview: Phoenix aims to bounce back vs. Clippers

Who: Phoenix Suns (3-6) vs. Los Angeles Clippers (2-7)

Where: Mortgage Matchup Center — Phoenix, Arizona

The Phoenix Suns will need to have a short memory after being dominated by Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs last night.

Wemby walked into our building and dropped 40, 11, and nine blocks in 25 minutes without breaking a sweat. Spurs 122, Suns 96. It was a rough night. But the silver lining is that the starters were on the bench with 9:34 left. Because tonight they have the second of a back-to-back, and tired legs cannot be an excuse.

The mood in this fanbase right now is somewhere between "burn it down" and "it's November, relax." The Suns sit at 3-6. They're 2-2 on this seven-game homestand. The two-game win streak over Houston and Orlando either becomes a distant memory (after a loss) or a building block if they win, because then it's suddenly "they've won 3 of their last 4 games". So which is it?

Make no mistake about it… this is a MUST-WIN game for the Suns. These are the teams you need to beat.

Ingram and Beal are still out, so expect LA to run back the same five that started Sunday in their win over the Pelicans.

Mark Williams — OUT (Left Shoulder Surgery)

Devin Booker needs help, and he needs it from the starters.

Book went 10-for-17 for 32 last night. The other four starters combined for 27 points on 10-of-36 shooting. That's 27.8%. Phoenix shot 39.3% as a team. Jalen Green, Dillon Brooks and Miles Bridges have to be the second and third options tonight, or this turns into another Booker solo show that ends in a loss.

LA snapped a seven-game skid Sunday by beating New Orleans 139-123, and the bench won that game: 59 points and 14 assists from the reserves. Gradey Dick went 6-for-7. Top-5 pick Keaton Wagler hit 3 of 4 from deep in 18 minutes. Wagler also picked up five fouls. That unit is 4th in bench scoring per game, but defensively they have some flaws. Attack, attack, attack.

Darius Garland went for 24 and 10 against the Pelicans. Brook Lopez added 20. Brandon Ingram (heel) and Bradley Beal (knee) are both out tonight. Gillespie, Goodwin and Green have to make Garland work on the ball, and whoever draws Lopez has to drag him out to the perimeter, where his feet are slow.

Rebounding is going to be the key for every Suns game, as the Spurs outrebounded them by twenty, 55 to 35.

LA shot 55% from the field (46 of 84), went 16-for-38 from three, and piled up 34 assists against 11 turnovers in their win over the Pelicans. They lived at the line, too: 31 of 38 from the line while the Pelicans committed 29 fouls. The glass was basically even, 36-35 Clippers, with LA grabbing 13 offensive boards.

The starters held serve, every one of them finishing between +2 and +9. The bench blew it open. Max Strus and Gradey Dick were both +17, Kobe Sanders was +15, and Keaton Wagler was +11. LA won the fourth quarter 37-28.

Collin Gillespie, anyone? It's been a rough season for him, and boy could they use a breakout game in this one from him, not only for his confidence, but to outduel the Clippers' bench. Jordan Goodwin is back as well, so that hopefully provides a spark.

Do not take them lightly. The Clippers are 2nd in the NBA in 3PT% and 4th in bench scoring. Despite their flaws and 7-game losing streak, they are fully capable of getting hot from deep and stealing this one.

The Suns bounce back, and their offense breaks out in a win over the Clippers. We enter the 10-game mark at 4-6, with mixed reviews, but ultimately trending in the right direction, winning 3 of 4.

#2739. Celtics’ Paul George hilariously gives 76ers fans the finger after dominant win

Celtics' Paul George hilariously gives 76ers fans the finger after dominant win appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

For all the talk about the simmering beef between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown, it was Paul George, the player the Boston Celtics acquired from the Philadelphia 76ers in the Brown trade, who proved to be the biggest star of the show. George finished with 36 points on 14-of-22 shooting from the field, and he hit some daggers in the fourth quarter to blow the game wide open en route to a 123-101 win over the 76ers.

In the fourth, it looks as though George was drawing inspiration from the animosity he was receiving from a few 76ers fans. In fact, during one pause in the action, the Celtics star subtly and hilariously gave a fan the middle finger just to rub it into their faces.

76ers fans are some of the most passionate in the world, and with the game getting out of hand in the fourth, getting George riled up did not help matters whatsoever.

After Payton Pritchard drained two straight threes to start the quarter to push the Celtics' lead to 15, George saw the opportunity to deliver the killing blows to the 76ers.

He pulled up for a triple to extend their lead to 18, and then he was clearly feeling himself as he drained a difficult turnaround and-one jumper and made the free throw to push their lead to 21. He would then score five more points to extend his personal run to eight, and by then, the 76ers were out of the game completely.

George is experiencing a career revival in Beantown; after his 36-point outing against his former team, he is now averaging 22.0 points, 5.2 rebounds, and 3.8 assists per contest on the year. He's also playing elite defense, and he looks like he's at least back to the form he showed during the latter part of his tenure with the Los Angeles Clippers.

Keeping him healthy is going to be key for the Celtics, as they are unstoppable when the 36-year-old forward is playing like this and even flipping opposing fans off in the process.

#2731. Penn State notes: Jack Ham remains in stable condition in Seattle hospital

Jack Ham, the Penn State football radio analyst and Pittsburgh Steelers legend, is making "great progress" at the University of Washington Medical Center, Nittany Lions coach Matt Campbell said Tuesday.

The 77-year-old Ham suffered a medical emergency shortly after arriving on a team bus Saturday at Husky Stadium for Penn State's Big Ten game against Washington.

"I talked to him a little bit (Monday) and talked to him a little bit today," Campbell said. "Number one, he's talking. He's in stable condition. He's still out in Washington. We got to see him after the game, which was awesome. He was doing really well.

"Again, I think that is great progress. We hopefully get him back here sooner than later."

A native of Johnstown, Ham has teamed with play-by-play man Steve Jones on Penn State's football radio broadcasts since 2000.

Ham played linebacker at Penn State from 1968-70 and helped the Lions finish 11-0 in back-to-back seasons (1968-69). He was a unanimous first-team All-American in 1970 and was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1990.

Ham went on to play 12 seasons (1971-82) for the Pittsburgh Steelers and helped them win four Super Bowl championships. He was voted to the All-Pro team nine straight years and inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988.

"I want to just say from my end a sincere thank you to so many people that have reached out," Campbell said. "What Jack and his family have meant to Penn State football, our program and the athletic department, we greatly appreciate the love and care that we have gotten on behalf of Jack."

Penn State still has not revealed what kind of emergency that Ham experienced.

Penn State wide receiver Koby Howard's recovery from an unspecified injury has been paused, according to Campbell.

Howard has missed the last six games because of an injury that Campbell said he suffered against Buffalo on Sept. 19.

"I think we kind of came to a decision a little bit (last) Thursday or Friday," he said. "We're kind of in a pause state right now on where Koby is at. We were trying to beat a timeline coming back.

"The reality is I've continued to say I refuse to put Koby on the field until he's 100% ready to go back on the football field. …We're in a pause state to make sure we get him fully 100% back to health."

Howard, a sophomore, caught 12 passes for 344 yards and two touchdowns in the first three games, averaging almost 28.7 yards per catch. He traveled with Penn State to Seattle for the Washington game and offered encouragement from the sideline.

"Watching how Koby has been involved, he's been an elite teammate," Campbell said. "Everybody is going to see how you led when it wasn't going well for you. It gives you the tools and that firepower when you do come back, you have the ability to use your voice in a powerful way. Koby is doing a great job."

Former safety Marcus Neal Jr. saw his first action at linebacker last week at Washington and had one solo tackle.

Neal started all 12 games last season at Iowa State and was one of three safeties to transfer to Penn State, along with Jeremiah Cooper and Jamison Patton. But he struggled and lost his starting role several weeks ago.

Campbell announced last month that he had been moved to linebacker.

"He's been taking reps at Will backer the past two or three weeks," defensive coordinator D'Anton Lynn said. "There's a lot of stuff that he does naturally well down there. He gets off blocks. He blitzes. He tackles. He plays downhill.

"There is some stuff that's different from a run-fit standpoint. It happens a lot quicker down there. The more reps he's gotten, the better he's gotten."

The Celtics visit the Philadelphia 76ers for the first of 4 games between them this season. They will meet in Philadelphia again on February 7. They will meet twice in Boston on January 21 and March 7. This is likely the most anticipated matchup of the season so far as there are many stories to watch in this game.

First, there is the beef, or the lamb chops and gravy, or whatever you want to call what has been going on between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown since the trade. In the preseason, as they were both warming up, they didn't even acknowledge each other. There has been a back and forth of words between them ever since. Also there is the story of Paul George returning to Philly for the first time and of Jaylen Brown and PG13 facing their former teams. There is also the story of the long time rivalry between the Celtics and 76ers and the teams who faced each other in the 2nd round of the playoffs last season.

There is also the story of the top 2 teams in the East facing off. The 8-2 Celtics are 2nd in the East with only Philadelphia (9-2) half a game ahead of them in the standings. The Celtics have won their last 3 games and the 76ers are looking for their 2nd straight win. The Celtics are 2-2 on the road while the 76ers are 4-2 at home. The Celtics won both games in the preseason. Both teams are 2-0 in games against division rivals.

The Celtics are playing in the first of back to back games. This is their 3rd back to back set this season already. They won the first game in both of their back to back sets this season. One win was at home while the other was on the road. The Celtics are 275-200 overall all time against the 76ers. They are 94-130 in games played in Philly. They tied the series 2-2 last season, with each team winning one at home and one on the road.

The 76ers made one of the biggest moves of the off season, trading Paul George to the Celtics to get Jaylen Brown. They also signed LeBron James, Dean Wade, Ariel Hukporti and Anfernee Simons as free agents. They drafted Labaron Philon, Jr with the 22nd pick in the draft. Along with Paul George, they lost Quentin Grimes, Kelly Oubre, Jr and Andre Drummond. Mike Gansey also replaced Daryl Morey as the 76ers' president of basketball operations.

After this game, the Celtics will complete their 4 game road trip with a game in Toronto in back to back games Wednesday. Then they play Dallas and Orlando at home before a West coast trip that takes them through Denver, Sacramento, Golden State, and Washington. They then play one game at home against Atlanta before playing at San Antonio and Dallas. Then it's home against Charlotte before a game at Brooklyn.

The 76ers will host Toronto and Indiana before road games at Brooklyn and Orlando. Then they host Milwaukee, Portland and Miami before games at Indiana and Houston. Then they have a 3 game home stand against Memphis, Denver and Orlando before playing at Orlando. Next they host Dallas and play at Charlotte. They will host Houston before a 5 game Western road trip.

The Celtics have been changing their starting lineup with Jordan Walsh, Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman, and Neemias Queta getting starts along with Derrick White, Paul George, Jayson Tatum and Mitchell Robinson. The starting lineup is a work in progress for the Celtics, especially the shooting guard spot that has changed pretty much from game to game. Move the Ball Carefully – The Celtics play the best when they move the ball and find the best shot. They struggle when they try to do too much individually. But, they have to be careful handling the ball and making passes. The 76ers are best in the league at taking care of the ball with just 12.9 turnovers per game. The Celtics are 12th with 14.9 turnovers per game. They have to stay focused and avoid turning the ball over.

X-FactorsOn the Road – The Celtics will be on the road once again for the 3rd straight game and they will be facing a very hostile crowd. Philly fans hate the Celtics because they have pretty much owned them in recent years. They hate Jayson Tatum because the Celtics took him with Philly's pick after the 76ers traded up to take Markelle Fultz. They now have another reason to hate the Celtics and that is to back up Jaylen Brown who has been very bitter against the Celtics and his former running mate. There will likely be a lot of boos and the Celtics need to play through them. They have to shake off the distractions of playing on the road and stay focused on playing Celtics basketball.. They can use the boos as motivation to play even harder.

Coaching – Joe Mazzulla is in his 5th season as Celtics' head coach. He won a title in 2024 with a very talented team that was packed with shooting stars. Now he has to win in a different way since his personnel has changed and so far he is doing a good job. Nick Nurse is in his 9th season as a head coach overall and his 4th as the 76ers head coach. He won a title with the Raptors in 2019. Nurse came out ahead in the playoffs last season. Can Mazzulla win this round?

Officiating – Officiating is always an x-factor in every game. Every crew officiates differently. Some call it tight, others let them play. The Celtics need to adjust to how the refs are calling the game and not allow bad calls or no calls to take away their focus from playing the game. The Celtics also have to be aware of the new points of emphasis for this season and try to avoid flopping, off‑arm push‑offs, reckless closeouts, delays before free throws, and illegal screens. They have been especially calling flops and push offs and so the Celtics need to make an effort to avoid doing both.

#2720. Injury pileup gets bigger: Brandon Williams out at least a week

Last night, Brandon Williams lasted just 99 seconds before sustaining an injury that kept him out the rest of the game. This afternoon, following an MRI, we've learned that it's a mild left hamstring strain that will keep him out for at least a week, which will be when he's next evaluated by the Golden State Warriors medical staff. It's a big blow for both the fifth-year vet and the team as this next 5-game stretch, already figuring to be the end of this historic winning streak at some point, could be a real setback.

As Brady mentioned last night, Williams joins Jimmy Butler III, Moses Moody, and Gary Payton II among the actively injured with Will Richard out indefinitely and Kristaps Porziņģis all but retired. That's 10 points, 2 rebounds, and 2 assists in 16 minutes a night that they'll have to make up in the near-term. It's not like solid backup point guards are easy to find, and the Dubs are already without a true center on top of all these injured forwards.

Still, it's worth wondering to what extent the team expected this. He had a bout of quad tightness a little over a week ago and was ruled out against the Suns; and as Anthony Slater noted earlier:

But left hamstring issues have followed Williams early in his NBA career. He strained it in the 2025 preseason while with Dallas and subsequently missed time last March while dealing with tightness.

The Warriors will need him back ASAP, but it's also early enough in the season where there's probably some incentive to let him take extra time to recover. All that to say that 7 days is probably the most optimistic recovery period. They're one of the trickiest injuries to deal with and it's probably easier to envision a far longer recovery period, especially since he had to come out of the game so suddenly.

So, the backup PG situation (non-Podziemski division) looks like this: De'Anthony Melton, Gui Santos, and LJ Cryer. Williams was a perfect change of pace. Like a shot of espresso off the bench. He provided such a jolt that that alone might be the hardest aspect of his game to reproduce in the aggregate.

#2719. Cy Ranch returns to Class 6A Division I state volleyball semifinals with win over Clear Springs

As Saniyah Reynolds rose above the net and hammered the final kill into the hardwood court at Delmar Fieldhouse, the celebration commenced for the Cypress Ranch volleyball team.

It had been 364 days since the Mustangs clinched their first appearance in the UIL state semifinals. Now they're starting to make it an annual tradition. Cy Ranch is headed back to the Class 6A Division I semifinals following a 25-21, 29-27, 25-17 victory against Clear Springs in the Region III final on Tuesday night.

"It's a special group," Cy Ranch coach Collea McKinney said. "I said that about last year, too, but these girls … I love our program from our girls all the way to our parents. It's definitely a community effort, and everybody coming together is what made this happen. I know we started building last year, but the girls this year got the see that, and they're like 'OK, that goal is attainable.' Now we're trying to go all the way, so I'm really excited."

HIGHLIGHT A GREAT ATHLETE: Nominate a Houston high school performer for Athlete of The Week

Cy Ranch (39-7) has won 28 consecutive matches since dropping four straight in tournament play at the end of August against some elite competition. The Mustangs suffered all seven of their losses within the first 18 matches of the season and have been lights-out since working through those growing pains. Entering Tuesday night, the six teams that had beaten the Mustangs boasted a combined .804 winning percentage. Cy Ranch has dropped just one set through the first four rounds of the playoffs, that coming during a win over Dawson in the regional semifinals.

"After last year, we were doubted a lot because we lost a lot of people," said junior outside hitter Sade Bello, a University of Kansas commit who entered the night with more than 600 kills after previously playing alongside her sister, Zora, a senior leader for last year's team. "But just knowing who we are and knowing who we have on this team, we know we can go as far as we did last year or even better if we can just stay disciplined and play our game."

Cy Ranch will play the Region IV champion, either Round Rock (35-11) or Lake Travis (41-6), at 4 p.m. Saturday back at Delmar Fieldhouse. Those teams were set to play each other later Tuesday. The Mustangs lost 2-0 against both earlier this season, but McKinney said her players are better now for some of the struggles they faced early on.

"I think a lot of growth happened during that time," McKinney said. "It was hard. The girls had to learn each other. During that time, it's pretty much a brand-new team if you look at our roster from last year to this year. They were learning how each other work, how to talk to each other and all the little things. As females, we have to learn to communicate properly in order to play together. During that time, they were going through that. I won't say we're best friends all the time, but I feel like we've learned how to play together and talk each other through those hard times. Those tough losses kind of shaped and molded them into the team they are now."

Clear Springs (38-10) saw its season come to an end after reaching a regional final for the first time in program history. After losing in the second round of the playoffs against Dawson last season, this year's Chargers were able push one victory further. Clear Springs has been a consistently strong program and has at least 29 wins in every season since 2021 under coach Shannon McClellen, who first took over the program in 2012.

The pivotal point of the match against Cy Ranch came in the second set. That set featured nine ties and saw the Mustangs stave off defeat after trailing 24-23. Cy Ranch then had four set points of its own before finally getting the final kill to win 29-27. From that point forward, the Mustangs had the momentum and closed out the match.

"Like I tell them all the time, we're better together," said McKinney, who has a 152-29 record at Cy Ranch since 2023. "We have a lot of great individuals on our team, so when we come together, I feel like we're unstoppable. And maybe I'm biased, and I should be I guess, but at the end of the day, they listened and they actually trusted each other. I think that's what made us get through that second set, because there were times in there where it got a little bleak. However, they didn't just lay down, and that's my biggest thing. We don't lay down for any loss."

Cy Ranch ultimately lost 3-0 against eventual state champion and MaxPreps national champion Byron Nelson in the semifinals last year, coming up just one victory short of advancing to Garland. This will be the second year the UIL has pre-determined sites for its state semifinal matches. Last season, Cy Ranch had to travel about four hours to Haltom City, near Fort Worth, for its matchup against Byron Nelson. This time around, the Mustangs have a significantly shorter trip back to Delmar after the realignment moved them from Region II to Region III.

Regardless of the venue, McKinney expects her team to be ready.

"No letdown ever," she said of the message to her players. "Know that you deserve to be here, and I'm going to be rooting for you the entire time. And they know that. Have each other's backs, and no letup … ever. That's our goal."

#2717. Jordan Poole would like to come home

The Golden State Warriors had a poignant reunion on Monday night, when they welcomed the New Orleans Pelicans to town, and proceeded to crush them by 51 points. There are a lot of former Warriors around the league, but some feel different when they face the Warriors, and that was the case when Jordan Poole checked into the game.

It's no secret that it's been a rough few years for Poole, whom the Warriors took with the 28th pick of the 2019 NBA Draft out of Michigan. After showing some signs in his first two seasons, Poole burst onto the scene during the 2021-22 campaign, when he became a starter, played 30 minutes a night, averaged 18.5 points and 4.0 assists, led the NBA in free throw percentage, had a highlight every game, and was at times the second option on a Warriors team that would eventually defeat the Boston Celtics to win an NBA championship.

But things went sideways for there. The next year was bittersweet, as Poole parlayed his performance into a massive extension, but was also on the receiving end of a punch from teammate Draymond Green, which led to uncomfortable vibes and thick tension for the entire year. The next offseason, the Warriors traded Poole to the Washington Wizards for Chris Paul, and, away from the confines of Steph Curry and Steve Kerr's offense, Poole struggled, putting up big numbers but on very low efficiency.

He bounced back with a strong offensive showing in 2024-25, but prior to last season was traded to the Pelicans. His first year in the bayou did not go according to plan, as he averaged just 13.4 points and shot a lowly 37.2% from the field.

This year has been even worse. Poole started the season slow, coming off the bench in the first four games of the season and having lackluster numbers. That earned him a benching, and when New Orleans came to town on Monday, Poole had gone six straight games without getting on the court.

That playing drought ended on Monday. With the Pelicans down a handful of key players — including Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III, and Yves Missi — and with the game a blowout from the start, Jamahl Mosley gave Poole his largest run of the season, playing him for 34 minutes. Poole didn't play well — he scored seven points on 1-for-5 shooting, with two assists and two turnovers — but it was still nice seeing him out there. And it was hard not to wonder: what could have been?

Maybe we'll get something of an answer someday. While Poole has been reluctant to discuss the situation with Green, Monday was the first time that he really spoke about his time in Golden State. And he didn't hide his feelings: he misses it.

Asked by reporters if he missed Golden State, Poole made his thoughts emphatically clear, saying, "Hell yeah! Obviously. They play the right way, bro. They play good basketball. They play team basketball … Do I miss it? Hell yeah."

Poole then spoke very openly about the difficulties of the current season, where he's struggling to find minutes on a team that is likely headed for the lottery. He didn't make excuses or cast blame anywhere, but repeated twice that the season — only a few weeks old — has been "pretty f*****g difficult."

His answer led to an obvious follow-up: would Poole, who will be an unrestricted free agent after the season, be amenable to a return to the Bay Area? Again, he left no doubt with his response, saying, "Yes. Yes. It just feels like home though, you know? Driving into the f*****g arena, crossing the Bay Bridge or wherever you're coming from, it definitely feels natural. And I think it's pretty evident, the way that I play is very fitting to how I used to play here. Nothing's changed, other than the systems that I'm in. We won a championship, you know, so it works … so to answer your question: definitely."

Poole elaborated, all but saying that he would jump at the opportunity to sign with the Dubs in free agency, should he be offered a contract. "I'm a free agent at the end of this season," the 27-year old explained. "If there's any place where I'm comfortable, it's probably where I started. So I just got to find ways to keep learning and try to make the best decisions for my future."

Barring something unexpected, the Warriors should have no problems finding the money to sign Poole next offseason, since his current play has tanked his value. A reunion would likely come down to whether or not the team felt they had a need for his services, and whether they believed he could bounce back following a few down years. He certainly seems like the ideal change-of-scenery candidate, and the Warriors are very familiar with his game and his work habits. They're always on the lookout for bench scorers, and especially could end up needing him if Brandon Williams departs next summer.

That's a long ways from now. But who knows: maybe this time next year, Poole will be back in a Warriors jersey. It sure sounds like he'd like that.
